51 is officially down another firefighter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Warning! Spoilers for Season 15, Episode 5 of Chicago Fire, “Three Hundred,” lie ahead.

Chicago Fire has had a revolving door of cast members over the 14 years it has been on the air. And unfortunately, that door is still spinning amid Season 15 on the 2026 TV schedule. Fans have already had to say goodbye to Dermot Mulroney’s Dom Pascal, but and that's not all. This week marked the NBC hit's 300th episode as well as the departure of Joe Cruz, played by OG cast member Joe Miñoso. While I was a mess watching Cruz’s farewell to 51, there were apparently “a lot of tears” on set, too, as Miñoso told me.

Following Season 14's cliffhanger, the Season 15 premiere revealed that no one at 51 died. However, Cruz broke his spine as a result of a collapse at the warehouse, and despite him doing extensive rehab, it would basically take a miracle for him to be a firefighter again. Wednesday’s episode, “Three Hundred,” saw Cruz getting the news that if he continued to do rehab and work hard, he could go back to work in a matter of months.

That being said, following the birth of his and Chloe’s twin girls, Cruz decided to take a step back and go to a great rehab facility in Minnesota close to Chloe’s parents. He had a very vulnerable chat with Severide about his decision, and his goodbyes with Hermann, Mouch, Tony, and Capp were equally emotional and funny. I definitely couldn’t stop crying while watching it, especially when Cruz stopped by Otis’ memorial and talked with his late friend. Unsurprisingly, Miñoso got emotional while filming his character's sendoff, and he spoke to CinemaBlend about the final scene he shot:

A lot of tears. The last scene that we did was with me and Taylor [Kinney], and it was where I'm explaining why I'm leaving. And so much of it felt really, kind of like true-to-life. It felt like a lot of things that Joe and Taylor would have said to each other, and it was such a, I think, you know, probably the most human and intimate scene that Taylor and I have ever had the opportunity to do.

Given Miñoso had been part of the cast since the very beginning, it's honestly got be hard to imagine Chicago Fire without him, and 51 without Cruz. It’s great, however, that he was able to have that opportunity with Taylor Kinney not only for their characters, who are basically brothers, but for themselves, too. That’s not the only reason it was emotional, though, as Miñoso will also have a core memory that lasts a lifetime:

It was, first and foremost, such a gift to be able to have that scene with him just because we've never really sat face-to-face as equals like that in a scene. It felt really special. The fact that it was the very last scene on the stage with my wife there, who I met on the show as a makeup artist 10 years ago, and we just celebrated our 10th anniversary. It'll be an implanted memory forever. It's like one of those core memories. It's definitely going to be one of the shining bright ones in my mind for a long time.

It was announced over the past summer that Miñoso would be leaving Chicago Fire, and many fans were not happy about it. That being said, the fact that Miñoso was able to be ushered out with five episodes to wrap up Cruz’s story makes it just a little bit more bearable.

Following the Season 14 cliffhanger, though, there was no telling what the result would be, and how it could figure into Cruz’s departure. Chicago Fire has killed off a handful of characters following season-ending cliffhangers. Luckily, when it came to how Cruz would bow out, there was only one way to handle it, per Miñoso:

There were a lot of discussions between the writers and producers and myself in terms of how we wanted to say goodbye to the character. But [showrunner] Victor [Teran] was pretty adamant from the very beginning that he wanted to be able to explore a different type of trauma on this show. We haven't really been able to play this storyline in terms of our firefighters getting so hurt that they can no longer be the person they think they are.

Cruz has been such a staple at 51, and his passion for the firehouse and his job trumped just about everything, aside from his family. With Miñoso leaving, it really only made sense for him to decide to leave 51 because of his family. And Miñoso loved the way it all came together:

But at some point, they overcome it and then ultimately make the decision to walk away on their own terms. So, it was really an honor, a joy, a privilege. I feel very lucky that they gave me the material and thought and believed in me to be able to bring it to life.

Character exits are always tough in the One Chicago franchise, especially when it’s someone who has been around since the start of a show. But since Cruz, Chloe, the boys, and now their baby twin girls are only a couple of states away, it’s possible that this won’t be the last we see of them. Nevertheless, I'll probably continue to be an absolute mess whenever I revisit this episode of the show.

If anything, all episodes of Chicago Fire are streaming with a Peacock subscription, so there is plenty of Cruz to still enjoy. As for new episodes, those air on Wednesdays at 9 p.m. ET on NBC.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

#3520. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3519. Meet Colleen Allen, the Future of American Fashion

This is the November 4, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

The United States has been overtaken by a blue wave following last night’s midterm elections. James Talarico flipped Texas to make it to the Senate, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia is now the first Black woman to be elected governor in the history of the US. There were great memes about what this could mean for the country—largely, the comeback of woke—and some fashion moments worth discussing. Scroll down for a midterm-fashion verdict, including notes on the curious case of a seemingly AI-generated picture featuring Chanel and Valentino products supposedly spotted at a Michigan Democratic Party election night event in support of Abdul El-Sayed.

In other news, Ye is staging a comeback Yeezy show in Los Angeles tonight at the brand’s flagship—keep an eye out tomorrow for a report from my Angeleno colleague Maxwell Adler. Congratulations are in order for Schiaparelli’s Daniel Roseberry, who is having a great week after running the New York City Marathon on Sunday, posting a much-discussed thirst trap on Monday morning, and receiving the Leader in the Arts Award at the Smithsonian’s annual Hirshhorn New York Gala on Monday night. Congratulations as well to the winners and honorees at the 2026 CFDA Awards. More on that very curious evening below, including an interview with Colleen Allen, certified fashion darling and Emerging Designer of the Year winner.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff and his tight suit, Colleen Allen, Ralph Lauren, Jill Biden, Melania Trump, Hasan Piker, Zohran Mamdani and Rama Duwaji, and Tim Burton and his new Loewe collaboration.

The CFDA Fashion Awards on Monday night brought some star power to the American Museum of Natural History: Keke Palmer hosted, and presenters included Matt Damon, Cole Escola, Lupita Nyong’o, Laufey, and Demi Moore. And yet the mood of the evening was somewhat tentative. The Council of Fashion Designers of America is under something of a renovation: Steven Kolb, its former CEO, resigned in September following an altercation with PETA protesters at New York Fashion Week. Serving in his stead is Hildy Kuryk, a comms expert who spent four years at Vogue as its executive director of communications following a career in politics. Kuryk is serving as interim CEO and heading up the search for Kolb’s permanent replacement. On Monday night, she stayed out of the spotlight, leaving most of the audience wondering—and gossiping about—who the new face of the CFDA could and should be.

Rachel Scott of Diotima took the main award of the night as womenswear designer of the year, and Anthony Vaccarello, who just left Saint Laurent, was presented with the International Designer of the Year Award by muses Zoë Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, and Rosé. Ralph Lauren was named menswear designer of the year, securing his place as the most awarded designer in CFDA history. Mr. Lauren himself made an appearance—a crowd-pleaser that also left me wondering if the American industry often puts too much emphasis on its past and not enough on its future. In that spirit, I called up Colleen Allen, who took the prize for emerging designer of the year, and asked her to introduce herself to those of you who haven’t met her yet.

Colleen Allen received her award from designer Gabriela Hearst and actor and writer Cole Escola.

José Criales-Unzueta: What would you say is the most important thing for people to know about your background?

Colleen Allen: I often lead with that I always was a menswear designer and was never intending on doing womenswear. That point of view has really guided my work and who I’ve become. I just love the process of making. I did menswear because there wasn’t an identity of women that I saw that I connected with, really, with brands when I was first going to school. And I just loved the craft of tailoring and learning the physical process of cutting a pattern. I think there’s such an ephemerality in making womenswear, in a way. Draping on a mannequin is quite abstract to me. A huge part of my identity is thinking like a tailor.

Where did you go to school, and where did you work before starting your brand?

I did half at Parsons, half at Central Saint Martins. I consider Parsons to be quite technical, and Saint Martins sort of opened up the world conceptually for me and gave me a lot of freedom and thinking about world-building. I was at The Row doing menswear for three years, and then I also interned at Vogue for a minute [and] Calvin Klein 205W39NYC was a very formative experience. When I was an intern there, I was full-time. I was there for eight months, but it was just so cool because it was all in the same room with Raf [Simons, now at Prada], Pieter [Mulier, now at Versace], Matthieu Blazy [now at Chanel]. You knew at that moment how special it was and how crazy it was. I think the world didn’t process it, but when you were in the room, you knew these people were all so important. And so I think being around that every day and absorbing the way that they worked together and they’re such world-builders, all three of them are very conceptual. I think that was a huge informative experience for me.

I think that people know me for color. The feedback that I get from people who buy the clothes is that when you’re wearing a big velvet coat in a color, or even just a dress or a top, people get stopped on the street just because it’s so visually impactful. Velvet is also a signature. That duality of color and texture, and also a bit of a historical Victorian sensibility.

Where do you think that interest in Victorian garments comes from?

There’s an emotional, aesthetic love for it. There’s a bit of a groundedness and a weight to it, and a bit of that period of time was quite spiritual thinking about the afterlife and death, but there was a sense of romance around that that I think really seeped into the clothes in a way that I don’t know if other periods of time really reflect. On the other side of it, it isn’t Victorian specifically, but a lot of historical dress for women is incredible tailoring—thinking about those bodice jackets that have a lot of tiny little panels with lots of little grosgrain finishing on the seams on the inside—and it’s all about molding to the female body. As a menswear designer, I love wearing men’s clothes and wearing a tailored jacket, but I think that the idea of having that sensibility and also reflecting femininity is the perfect storm for me. A lot of that just got lost in a certain period of time once women were able to wear pants, and in the transition of women being able to access menswear, women’s tailoring never got back to that sort of technical level of fitting the body or the female form.

You’ve never done a runway show, which is something that many young designers feel signals their arrival. Why is that?

I love fashion and wanted to work in fashion because I loved watching fashion shows. And specifically, I loved shows that were immersive. I always go back to [Alexander] McQueen [that signaled] fashion is more than product. It is this world-building, cinematic performance art, and you can take it just so much further emotionally. If I’m going to do a show, I want it to carry that level of weight. For me, at my scale, it just feels like the most manageable way to encapsulate a sense of emotion is to do it through a [photo] shoot and showroom appointments for now, just in truly a practical sense. But it is my dream, and I’m working towards having a show. But when I do it, I want it to feel special.

It’s a bit surreal, in a way. It’s especially cool that it’s voted by the industry, and it sounds maybe kind of cheesy, but I do just feel like that is the best reward. That all these people that I’ve worked with are acknowledging [me]. It feels solidifying, grounding. It feels like I’ve been doing this forever, and it’s also going by so fast at the same exact time. It lets me be present and acknowledge myself for how much work has been put into it and that I did it and it’s real and it’s something I dreamed about for so long.

Do you feel like a fashion-industry darling?

[Laugh] Oh my God, how does one answer that question? Gosh, I think that three years ago I was entering these rooms knowing absolutely no one... I think the showroom has actually really fostered real relationships and friendships in the industry, and a sense of community that just feels really good. I work as hard as I can to support whatever the stylists are doing or the editors, I’m always physically running around to make sure that they get the clothes because I love what they do. I love that I know the photographer and the stylist and all the people, and know that if my clothes are in it, it will be amazing for me and they made the effort to reach out to me, to include me in it. The word darling is such an ick word [laugh]. I feel like the word I want to say is camaraderie, because everyone just works so hard. Nobody is flouncing around being a darling. We are all hustling together, and if I can support your hustle and you support mine, that’s the best thing. And when it works, it’s just so satisfying.

Tim Burton, iconoclast filmmaker extraordinaire, has a new capsule with Loewe, which has recreated characters and vignettes from The Nightmare Before Christmas as bags and charms. These kinds of collabs were a staple when Jonathan Anderson was at the brand, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez seem to be game to keep them coming with the same endearing whimsy.

In the age of artificial intelligence, the film has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton told me yesterday, calling from London and answering a question about the proliferation of AI in film, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.” We also spoke about his collaboration with A$AP Rocky and whether he’d ever do a live-action remake of 2005’s Corpse Bride.

#3518. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3517. Ganondorf's Castle dungeon walkthrough in Ocarina of Time

Ganondorf's Castle is the final dungeon in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and you'll need to use everything you've learned from the previous dungeons to reach Ganondorf and save Princess Zelda.

There will be six rooms, with each one representing one of the elements. You'll need to solve the puzzle in each room in order to destroy the barrier protecting the central tower. However, the puzzles can get a bit tricky, and you might need a refresher on how some mechanics work.

Here's howw to complete Ganondorf's Castle and defeat him once and for all.

Head into Ganondorf's Castle, which used to be Hyrule Castle, and blow up the two Beamos down the hall. Head through the door, and you'll enter the main room inside Ganondorf's Castle. To progress, you need to destroy the six barriers blocking off the central tower. Each barrier corresponds to one of the temples. The Fire and Light doors are blocked off with black and gold blocks, so you can't go in those right away.

Before you head into any of the rooms, go under the bridge leading to the central tower. Put on the Lenses of Truth, and look at the wall to find a hidden entrance to a Fairy fountain. Come back here if you ever need to heal, or you can bottle a fairy now.

You can technically go into any of the open doors, but first, make your way to the Shadow room, which can be found behind the central pillar. We're sending you to the Shadow room first, because you'll find an important item inside.

Light the unlit torch on the pillar, and a bunch of platforms will rise from the ground. The platforms won't stay up forever, so you'll have to move quickly. If you need arrows, go to the chest on the side. If not, cross the platforms to the larger platform on the other side of the room.

Defeat the Like Like, and use your Hover Boots to cross over to the next platform. Put on the Lenses of Truth to spot a path to the button on your right. Step on it, and a chest containing the Golden Gauntlets will appear. These gauntlets will let you pick up the huge black and gold rock on the left side of the chest. Interact with the rock, and Link will automatically throw it into the pit.

Follow the path ahead and step on the button, which will unlock the door to the next room. Put on the Lenses of Truth, and you'll see a floating platform. Use your Hover Boots to reach it, and then make your way to the next room.

In this room, you'll find a mysterious bulb that is emitting dark energy. Equip the Light Arrows that Zelda gave you, and shoot an arrow at the bulb. Impa will appear and tell you that you need to save the princess, sending you back to the main room in the process.

Now, you're free to enter the rooms in any order you'd like, but first, we recommend exiting Ganon's Castle and throwing the black and gold rock just across the bridge. This will reveal the entrance to a Great Fairy Fountain, where you'll receive the Gift of Halved Damage. This will halve all damage taken, and you can get it as long as you offer 500 rupees to the fountain.

You're free to go into any room, but for this guide, we'll just be going counterclockwise from the entrance.

Head inside the Forest door, which is on your right. In this room, you'll find a Wolfos and five unlit torches (four in the center and one above the locked door). Defeat the Wolfos and use either Din's Fire or Fire Arrows to light the torches.

Go into the next room, which is a crystal room. You'll find a fan in each corner and a Beamos in the center of the room. Walk over to the left, and you'll spot a time sigil on the wall. Play the Song of Time (A - L - R- A - L - R) and a time cube will appear. Jump over to it, collect the crystal, and put on your Hover Boots before the wind blows again. Take out the Beamos, and use your Hover Boots to reach the button. Longshot to the target that rises, and collect the crystal above it. Then, use your Hover Boots to collect the remaining three crystals.

Head into the next room to find a mysterious pulsating bulb that is emitting dark energy. Equip your Fairy Bow with Light Arrows and shoot it. The barrier will fall and Saria will appear. She'll give you some motivational words before you teleport back to the main room.

Next, head into the Water room, but be careful as two Freezards will spawn as soon as you enter. If you have Fire Arrows, you can use them to melt the Freezards in one hit. Otherwise, avoid their icy breath and take them out. Break the ice stalagmites surrounding the blue fire in the center of the room. Bottle some blue fire and use it to melt the red ice. Bottle up some more blue fire for the next room. Also, don't try to open the chest on the left side of the room, because it's fake!

Go into the next room, and you'll find two movable ice blocks, like the one from the Ice Cavern. Push the farthest block to the right, into the mound of ice. Then, push it into the hole. Push the other ice block over the ice block that fell in the hole and into the ice mound. Then, push it into the other ice mound, and finally, push it toward the red ice. Melt the red ice and hit the button with the Megaton Hammer to unlock the door.

Hit the bulb with a Light Arrow, Ruto will tell you the usual spiel about helping Zelda, and you'll get teleported back to the main room.

Head to the Fire room and throw the giant black and gold rock out of the way. Equip the Goron Tunic and go inside. This is another room where you have to collect five crystals. Three can be found on the right side of the room, while the other two are on the left. However, as soon as you step onto the winding platforms, they'll all slowly sink into the lava. Quickly run to each crystal to avoid sinking. To get every crystal, you need to throw the black and gold rock into the stalactite. It'll fall into the lava and make a platform to reach one of the crystals.

After you've collected every crystal, Longshot to the door and head into the next room to find the beating bulb again. Hit it with a Light Arrow, and you'll meet your brother Darunia, who will send you back to the main room.

Throw the rock blocking the Light room, and head inside. Equip the Lenses of Truth to spot a few invisible Keese on the walls and the invisible Skulltula hanging from the ceiling. Take them out first to unlock the door and spawn a chest containing a red rupee in the center of the room. Then, spot the moving chests around the room. Don't open them, but hit them instead. Afterwards, you're free to open the other chests, which will all have a blue rupee.

Go into the next room, and use the Lenses of Truth to find the invisible chest on the left side of the room. Open it to get a small key. If you'd like a green rupee, play Zelda's Lullaby (Y - X - A - Y - X - A) on the Triforce to spawn a chest with one inside. Use the small key to open the door to the next room.

Inside this room, you need to collect all five crystals, but there are a couple rolling boulders that you need to look out for. Follow a boulder and pick up the crystals as you run around the room. After you've picked up four, stand in one of the alcoves and look at the ceiling in the center of the room. Longshot to the target, and grab the last crystal on the center platform.

Head into the next room, only to realize that the bulb is missing. A spotlight will form on top of you, meaning a Wallmaster will shortly drop onto the ground. Avoid them and take them out. Then, put on the Lenses of Truth to see the bulb through a fake wall. Go through and hit it with a Light Arrow. Rauru will appear and send you back to the main room.

Go into the Spirit room, and you'll find a bunch of statues, Blade Traps, and a Beamos. This room is also another crystal room, so you'll have to grab the five crystals to unlock the next door. Move the statues so that the Blade Traps have more space to move, which also means you'll have more time to collect the crystals. However, the statue in the far left corner is actually an Armos, so keep your Megaton Hammer ready to whack them.

After you collect the crystals, head into the next room, where you'll be greeted with two Torch Slugs in front of a mesh wall. Hit them with your Megaton Hammer to make quick work of them, and a chest containing a Business Scrub seed will appear on your right. If you look through the mesh wall, you'll see a diamond-shaped switch, and if you look above the wall, you'll see a hole. Get as close to the wall as you can, and quickly release a Bombchu. It'll crawl through the hole and blow up right next to the switch, unlocking the door to the next room.

Go to the next room, and you'll see a spider web on the ceiling and suns on the wall. Hit the spider web with a Fire Arrow or Din's Fire, and sunlight will come through the hole in the ceiling. Reflect the light onto the sun to the right of the doorway you just came through. You'll see that the sun is filling up with green light, and then the door will unlock. Don't reflect the light onto any of the suns that fill up with red light, or else a Floormaster or a Wallmaster will spawn.

Head through the unlocked door, and shoot the bulb with a Light Arrow to break the barrier.

Make your way into the central tower, and ride the elevator to the next floor. Follow the path ahead, defeat the Fire Keese, and go through the door. You'll enter a room with two Dinolfos. Wait for them to jump at you, dodge to the side, and get a few hits in. Repeat this until you defeat them both, and the door to the next room will unlock.

Follow the path to the next room, where you'll take on two Stalfos. Watch out for their sword to flash, as that means they're about to do a jump attack. Hop to the side and attack them until you defeat them both.

Head to the next room, where you'll have to take on two Iron Knuckles, but you only have to wake up one at a time. Backflip away from their side sweeping attack, and jump to the side when they slam their axe in front of them. If you do get hit by an attack, make them destroy their thrones, and three hearts will drop. After you destroy the armor on one Iron Knuckle, the other will wake up, so do your best to quickly take out the first Iron Knuckle. Once you defeat both, a chest containing the boss key will spawn.

Continue along the path, and you'll enter a room with a bunch of climbable surfaces. Go through the door and up the stairs to find the boss room door.

Before you face off against the Great Demon King, Ganondorf, there are a few things you should know about the fight:

At the start of the fight, Ganondorf will slam onto the ground, causing the floor around the center of the room to drop. Then, he'll charge up a magic orb and throw it at you. You need to hit it with your sword to reflect it back at him, but he'll also hit it back, so you'll be in a rally for a bit. After you reflect the ball three times, Ganondorf will charge up his fist and punch the ball a little harder than usual, making the ball faster. Get ready to hit the orb at a faster cadence whenever this happens.

After Ganondorf misses his return and gets hit by the orb, his chest will glow and emit dark energy, similar to the bulbs inside the rooms downstairs. Hit his chest with a Light Arrow, and he'll drop to the floor. Then, jump over to the central platform and hit Ganondorf as many times as you can.

Ganondorf will slam onto the ground again, causing a few floor tiles to fall. He'll throw another ball at you, and the fight will start to repeat. However, your rallies with Ganondorf will get longer, and he'll incorporate new attacks:

Eventually, only the floor tiles in the corners of the room will be left standing. Continue to reflect the orbs at him and avoid his other attacks until he becomes vulnerable again. Longshot to the climbable wall on the center platform, and climb up to attack him. Repeat this process until you defeat him.

After you defeat Ganondorf, Zelda will be free, but the castle will begin to collapse. Run down the stairs with Zelda either past her or by her side, and she'll eventually unlock the the door at the bottom.

Take the path to the left and make sure to jump across the gaps in the floor. You'll eventually reach another locked door that Zelda will unlock. Inside, you'll face off against two Stalfos. Defeat them and Zelda will run on ahead. Follow her and Longshot onto the target to cross the gap with Zelda.

Continue into the next room, where the floor will break, and you'll drop into the room below. Zelda will hold off the incoming enemies, and you need to find a way out. Look away from Zelda, and you'll see a rock wall on the left side of the fire. Break it to reveal a way out. Follow the path, and you'll run into a bunch of ReDead. Zelda will lock them in place with her magic. Run into the middle of the pack and do a spin attack to defeat them.

Zelda will unlock the next door, and the tower will collapse. You'll successfully make it out, but there will be a loud noise in the distance. I wonder who it might be...

Before you walk over to the pile of rubble, there are a few things you should know about the fight against Ganon:

For the first part of the fight, Ganon has one weak spot: his tail. As you don't have the Master Sword, you need to use your items to damage it, but you'll need to wait for Ganon to attack, which will give you enough time to retaliate.

Ganon has three different attacks to look out for:

After Ganon slams his sword into the ground, his sword will be stuck in the ground for a bit. Quickly run behind him and attack his tail with the Megaton Hammer or the Fairy Bow.

When Ganon lifts his sword, you can shoot an arrow between his legs to hit his tail. You'll only have a brief moment to shoot the arrow though, so be ready! Alternatively, you can try to throw a Bombchu between his legs and have it explode next to his tail. But, this is a little tricky as you'll need to time it properly.

For Ganon's jumping attack, keep some distance to avoid getting smushed. Then, wait for his next move. Continue to attack his tail until it breaks, and the fight will move on to the second phase. Zelda will throw the Master Sword back to you, but Ganon will gain a third eye and his arms will start to glow. Fortunately, his third eye will close and you'll also gain a buff of your own as the Master Sword starts to glow.

For the second part of the fight, Ganon's attacks will largely mirror his attacks from the first phase, but this time, circles will form on the ground and lightning will strike in the same location shortly after. These circles will appear as he's winding up an attack and after he swings his sword, so make sure to avoid them.

To deal damage to Ganon, you need to hit his arms with the Master Sword or Light Arrows. The only opportunity to use the Master Sword will be when Ganon's sword is stuck in the ground, so use your Light Arrows to damage his arms whenever you can. After you've dealt enough damage, his empowered arms will explode and revert to normal.

Once both of Ganon's arms have been destroyed, he'll enshroud himself in dark energy and start charging at you. Keep your distance and constantly move around the edge of the arena to avoid getting hit. Eventually, Zelda will cast magic, causing Ganon's third eye to open.

For the third part of the fight, Ganon's attacks will still be roughly the same, but now when he slams the ground, multiple ruptures will form rather than just one. However, there's a lot of space between the ruptures, so you can stand between them and you'll be safe.

Ganon's weak spot during this phase is his third eye. Shoot a Light Arrow at it whenever you can. He'll cover it just before he's about to attack, but it'll be out in the open at every other moment. After you shoot his eye three times, he'll drop to the ground, and you can attack his eye with the Master Sword, defeating him.

The Sages will use their power to seal him away, and you'll finally defeat Ganon once and for all. Watch the rest of the cutscenes, and you'll reach the end of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3516. New Dunkin' Donuts Commercial Explains The Biggest Threat The Avengers Face In Doomsday

Marvel Cinematic Universe die-hards might have a more complete understanding of what awaits in "Avengers: Doomsday," but the average viewer just knows the Avengers are going up against Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom. Now, however, a wise sage has arrived to explain the plot of the upcoming superhero team up: Dunkin' Donuts. A new commercial for the company's Marvel Studios collab, available on YouTube, sees Channing Tatum's Gambit laying out the premise of "Doomsday" with the help of the Fantastic Four's H.E.R.B.I.E. in the most straightforward way possible.

"Doomsday" takes place fourteen months after the events of "Thunderbolts*," and sees three groups of heroes team up to take on Doctor Doom. Just what Doom is up to in the movie remains somewhat unclear at this point. Thus far, the "Doomsday" trailers have mainly focused on hyping up Doom's arrival and the return of beloved characters from MCU history. We do know the Avengers, New Avengers, Wakandans, Fantastic Four, and the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men will be putting up a united front against RDJ's villain, but otherwise we're eagerly awaiting the film's December 18, 2026 release to find out just how he fits into the story.

In the meantime, Channing's Gambit and H.E.R.B.I.E. (Humanoid Experimental Robot, B-Type, Integrated Electronics) are here to offer a simplified explanation of the existential threat facing the MCU. Marvel has teamed up with Dunkin' to deliver a new range of treats that look at once delicious and capable of dissolving your insides in a matter of seconds. Turns out, these new menu items are also pretty handy for explaining the impending collapse of the multiverse.

In the Dunkin' promo clip, entitled "Incoming Munchkins Incursion!" H.E.R.B.I.E. and Gambit are seen in Avengers Tower. The robot points out the window at a planet seemingly on a collision course with the one on which he and Gambit sit. He then uses two donut hole Munchkin treats to represent worlds colliding with one another, in what's known as an incursion, thus explaining the core problem at the heart of "Avengers: Doomsday" more clearly and succinctly than any of the trailers so far.

We first learned about incursions in the sort of fun Sam Raimi movie "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," wherein John Krasinski's Reed Richards explained how "an incursion occurs when the boundary between two universes erodes, destroying one or both entirely." In "Doomsday," it seems multiple incursions are happening at the same time, threatening the existence of the entire multiverse. As various universes collide with one another, characters from different timelines (i.e. different eras of Marvel's cinematic history) come into contact, hence why "Doomsday" features characters from so many different films. We sort of knew "Doomsday" would feature multiple incursions, given the events of films leading up to the movie. But the Dunkin' commercial makes it about as clear as possible.

That said, in the commercial, Gambit appears to be in Avengers tower, which means he's almost certainly on Earth 616 in the main MCU timeline. But when H.E.R.B.I.E. points to the planet in the sky, Gambit says "That's our world, there?" Channing Tatum has confirmed his Gambit is from the same world as the Fox-era X-Men. So when Gambit says, "That's our world there," is he talking about the Fox-era universe? Or H.E.R.B.I.E. and the Fantastic Four's universe? Likely the former, but it isn't entirely clear.

Channing Tatum was originally supposed to lead a Gambit movie during the 20th Century Fox X-Men era. But Tatum's Gambit movie failed after the studio tried to make it a comedy and once Disney bought the studio, it seemed that was the end of the whole thing. Tatum thought he'd lost Gambit forever before "Deadpool & Wolverine" came along and gave him a chance to finally debut as Remy Etienne LeBeau, the New Orleans native with the power to manipulate kinetic energy.

But Tatum's Gambit accent created a hilarious problem on "Deadpool & Wolverine." Because the movie was infused with the irreverent comedy of Ryan Reynolds' previous Deadpool outings, Gambit was made to use a heavy Cajun accent that essentially made him unintelligible — a joke that caused his co-stars to crack up on-set. But it seems he'll be toning down the accent for "Doomsday," as evidenced by the Dunkin' commercial.

The actor previously told Variety, "I'm not gonna go full Cajun. [Directors Anthony and Joe Russo] want things to be funny, but they don't want to go full 'Deadpool.' They want to keep the drama and keep it tight." This Dunkin' commercial is the first time we've been able to hear just how Tatum's new Gambit accent will sound, and it's certainly more intelligible than in "Deadpool & Wolverine."

Otherwise, "Avengers: Doomsday" is shaping up to be a tumultuous moment for the MCU, both on and off-screen, with Marvel Studios attempting to bring audiences back on board following a less than impressive Multiverse Saga. We'll have to see how it all pans out when the movie hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3515. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3514. Star Trek Cast A Real-Life American Hero In The Perfect Role

In the image above, you'll see real-life Georgian politician Stacey Abrams, the minority leader of the state's House of Representatives from 2011 through 2017. She played the president of a united Earth in a notable 2022 episode of "Star Trek: Discovery."

The final episode of the fourth season of "Discovery" was called "Coming Home," and it wrapped up a story arc involving the mysterious Species 10-C, an alien species so cognitively and physiologically different from average humanoids that communication proved near-impossible. The species was so different, in fact, it took months of research to get them right.

Species 10-C was responsible for unleashing a widespread gravitational cataclysm called the Dark Matter Anomaly, which was unwittingly poised to do untold destruction on Earth and other worlds. A lot of diplomacy and panic were involved in trying to contact Species 10-C and explain to them what they were doing. /Film reviewed the season, and found it to be a tricky balance between the cosmic and the personal.

Throughout the season, there is chatter about evacuating Earth, and mention of the planet's president. In the 32nd century, when "Discovery" takes place, Earth will still be united, and will have a singular presidential figure overseeing its government. The president appears at the end of "Coming Home" to put a button on the whole season, reiterating that communication and diplomacy are very, very good indeed. It's wholly fitting that a real-life politician like Stacey Abrams should be willing to appear as that character.

Abrams famously ran for governor of Georgia in 2018, but narrowly lost to Republican Brian Kemp. She ran again in 2022, but lost to Kemp a second time. She has long been an outspoken advocate for voting rights, and founded the organization Fair Fight Action, which aims to fight against voter suppression. She's quite well-suited to appear in the futuristic utopia of "Star Trek."

The end of "Coming Home" involves Earth rejoining the United Federation of Planets, an organization that had fallen by the wayside in the previous few centuries. Stacey Abrams has a scene with Captain Michael Burnham (Sonequa Martin-Green), the show's lead character in which the President of United Earth is presented as somewhat regal, although Abrams, not an actress, brings a grounded officiousness to the role as well. When she says, "United Earth is ready right now to rejoin the Federation, and nothing could make me happier than to say those words," it sounds like a speech that a 21st-century Earth politician might say.

Martin-Green was blown away to be working with Abrams, something she gushed about in an interview with Deadline. She said:

"I'm still floored when I think about Stacey gracing us with her presence in our Season 4 finale. [...] We spent so much of our time fanning out and pretending to be cool in her midst. [...] She's a legend in the making and a civil hero, and she was an absolute delight to work with. [...] She wowed us with her charm, humility, and generosity, and she whipped out some acting chops too! [...] It was an honor for me as a Black woman to stand with her in the story. It's an experience I'll cherish for the rest of my life."

Abrams is cherished throughout the American political landscape. In 2019, she was selected to deliver the response to the President's State of the Union address, and she was even buzzed about as a potential running mate for presidential candidate Joe Biden. The New York Times cited Abrams as a major influence on boosting voter turnout in her state.

Stacey Abrams seems to believe that everyone should have a voice in American elections, which is a philosophy that falls very neatly in line with the overall egalitarian thinking behind "Star Trek." If anyone was to be present for Earth to rejoin the Federation, Abrams certainly fit the bill.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, Abrams has long been a fan of "Star Trek," and was well aware of the rise of Captain Michael Burnham. Abrams wanted to be involved in "Star Trek: Discovery" no matter what plotline was being explored. She posted a video to her Twitter/X account, and was quoted as saying:

"Whatever the story was, I wanted to be a part of it because watching Michael Burnham come into her power as captain, watching this party-crew reclaim itself — not only in a new era but in a new space that is so reminiscent of what they remembered but so different — that, to me, speaks of why we do the work we do in politics. [...] It's about giving people hope and giving them a better life and creating this vision of what is possible."

Abrams has long stood up for justice, fairness, and equality. #3513. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3512. This Cult Sci-Fi Horror Series With Stephen King Vibes Has Become A Major Netflix Hit

There are so many problems with streaming media, but a big one is that each of these companies is hellbent on creating new movies and shows to fill out their library of licensable titles. There's a lot that's worth watching, but there's nowhere near enough time to watch these worthy works. As a result, great films and series fall between the cracks or get unceremoniously cancelled before they can complete their run.

So it's something of a miracle that "From," a science fiction horror series created by John Griffin that flew under the radar for several years, survived for five seasons. The final season was greenlit by MGM+ last April, thanks in large part to the show's enthusiastic cult following, but the company might consider lobbying Griffin for another season. Because this cult favorite has become a bona fide hit on Netflix.

Netflix began streaming the first three seasons of "From" last month, and it's currently the fourth most popular series on the service. It's not hard to understand why. Griffin's show is basically "Lost" with major Stephen King vibes, and it even features one of the show's stars, Harold Perrineau.

"From" opens with a family of four being forced to re-route their road trip when their chosen path is blocked by a fallen tree. They wind up in a small town where they receive directions out of the area from Sheriff Boyd Stevens (Perrineau), but they soon find themselves back in the town again. Gradually, they discover that there is no escaping this unnamed town.

"From" quickly makes "Lost" look like a lovely tropical vacation when it's revealed that the town turns decidedly lethal at night, due to the presence of vicious, human-looking monsters. And the show is unsparing in depicting these creatures' savagery. It's a gorehound's delight.

A major reason why "From" never caught on with mainstream viewers is that the first season streamed on Epix, which would eventually be acquired by MGM+. So Netflix is essentially doing a huge favor for MGM+, because "From" is every bit as addictive as "Lost."

Given the series' uptick in visibility, perhaps the critically acclaimed show (all four seasons rate over 90% on Rotten Tomatoes) will finally earn some Primetime Emmy nominations. It won the Saturn Award for Best Horror Television Series last year, and Perrineau is well overdue for Emmy consideration. The only impediment here is that voters will have to binge four seasons of a show that was off their radar.

If voters do take the plunge, they'll find a smart, terrifying series that flirts with the bleakness of Stephen King's legendary horror bummer "The Mist." A lot of people may not have the stomach for that, but Griffin and his writers adroitly plumb the darkness of our era, where days often feel like a purgatorial drag. But "From" keeps us watching because we need to believe there's a way out of this.

#3511. Apple confirms iOS 27.3 beta is coming next week with Apple Intelligence in China

Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details.

In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country.

Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features.

The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October.

Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year.

However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being.

While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize.

Now, as spotted by MacRumors, a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta.

Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself.

In the press release, Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself.

The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple.

Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others.

Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese.

The company also confirmed that the features will become publicly available in December, with the official release of iOS 27.3.

#3510. 10 Ocarina of Time beginner's tips that will save you some time

The original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a tricky and difficult game, especially so when it first came out. The Ocarina of Time remake follows in the same footsteps, but just a bit more modernized. Some puzzles and quests are a tad easier now, but that doesn't mean you'll have a nice stroll through the Lost Woods. Ocarina of Time is still a challenging game that will put your brain to the test.

Here are 10 beginner's tips and tricks to help you on your journey across Hyrule.

Before you start exploring, head into your settings and adjust them to your liking. You can change how fast the camera moves, turn off motion-control aiming, swap jump from X to B, simplify your HUD, and more. It's best to change all of these settings as soon as you start playing, so you don't acclimate to the original settings.

If you didn't play the original Ocarina of Time, this may seem a bit trivial as every game has some way to sprint and jump. However, in the original, players would constantly forward roll to move faster and let the game do the jumping for them. Luckily, the Ocarina of Time remake has been modernized a tad.

To sprint, press A once and then hold it down. Unfortunately, you can't adjust it to be a toggle, but at least you don't have to mash A anymore. To jump, press X, but you can also adjust it to B in the settings. It's also important to note that you can jump attack, which will deal double damage.

When you encounter new monsters and enemies, wait for Navi to fly over them and press Right on the D-pad. Navi will tell you what the creature is, and sometimes, she'll give you tips on how to beat them or even their weakness.

As you travel to new areas in Ocarina of Time, it can be hard to figure out what you should do first to progress. Talk to the townspeople and guards, and they'll provide you with little snippets of what's happening in the area. However, sometimes they'll tell you that you should avoid certain dangerous areas, but you're the Hero of Time! Sometimes you can and should ignore the townspeoples' advice and head straight into danger.

Fairy Thoughts are, well, a fairy's thoughts scribbled onto a surface. You can find them on walls and trees all around Hyrule. Make sure to read them, because they'll tell you about secrets hidden around the area.

Like in every RPG, you'll accumulate a bunch of items. In Ocarina of Time, you'll have a bunch of bombs, Deku nuts, arrows, magic power, and more. Make sure to actually use these items rather than horde them. It's very easy to get more of these items and resources as every blade of grass, every flower, and every tree has a chance of dropping them.

As you progress through the story, you'll accumulate multiple bottles that you can store things in. Fill up your bottles with bugs, red potions, fairies, Lon Lon Milk, or literally anything that you can as you explore. You never know when you'll find a pile of soft soil that needs a bug or if you'll encounter a dire situation where you need to restore a few hearts. Additionally, if you know you're going to enter a dungeon, stock up on some healing items!

You'll come across many interesting-looking things that you can't interact with. In due time, as you complete dungeons and progress in the story, you'll unlock more key items and abilities. This does mean you'll need to revisit areas that you've already been to, but you'll be rewarded with more secrets and collectibles that are worth your while if you do.

And I mean that literally. Ocarina of Time is full of helpful sound cues. You'll hear Skulltulas and Gold Skulltulas skittering about, ominous noises when an enemy is targeting you, icicles cracking just as they're about to fall, and, most importantly, delightful music in each area. The sounds you hear will help you progress through dungeons and solve difficult puzzles.

Zelda Notes is a feature on the Nintendo Switch App that has quizzes, your play data, the Threads of Time, and even additional quests. However, the most useful feature is its map, as it'll track your location in game in real time and show you the locations of collectibles.

Before you use it though, it's important to note that the app can and will show you spoilers for Ocarina of Time, so it might be best to play through the game first, especially if it's your first time playing. Whenever you're ready to use Zelda Notes, make sure to head to the Settings and enable it. Then, download the Nintendo Switch App on your mobile device, and link your account. As soon as you walk out of your house, the app will be good to go.
