#3484. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3483. ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release the film in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

When Siân Heder’s “CODA” premiered at Sundance in 2021 (during the festival’s online-only “pandemic year” and months and months before the film would go on to win Best Picture), it became an early favorite of mine. Mostly, I wrote in my review, though the “drama is marked by familiar beats, its characters bring new dimension to a staid genre.” The same can be said about Heder’s follow-up feature, “Being Heumann,” which brings real life back to the biopic, not only through innumerable compelling characters, but the smart choice to tightly focus this story on one essential moment in the life of the activist Judy Heumann. Related Stories Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com

When we first meet Judy (Ruth Madeley in a true star turn), she’s zipping along a busy New York City street in 1972. That might sound fun, but for Judy, it’s just the way things are; a wheelchair user since she was just a toddler (thanks to an early bout with polio), the world is not made for people like Judy, and she makes her way through it however she can. Often, that means doing things like, oh, zipping down city streets, because there are no curb cuts to assist her in smoothly moving from sidewalk to sidewalk. As Judy goes barreling down the street, people stare, drivers yell, and the brassy Brooklynite throws up a finger.

That Judy has natural presence is a given, but the central question of Heder’s film — which she adapted from Heumann’s autobiography alongside co-writer Rebekah Taussig — is how she will use all that verve to truly enact change. It’s the sort of concern that has always impacted great leaders, and suffice it to say, Heumann was indeed a great leader. But while Heumann’s long, storied life had many incredible chapters (she passed away in 2023, two years after she started working with Heder on the film), the filmmakers smartly zero in one on seminal slice of life to craft “Being Heumann.” Cradle to the grave this is not, but the film still succeeds mightily when contextualizing Heumann’s role in the disability rights movement and her singularity as a true American original.

That’s not to say that the period of time covered by the film — which soon jumps ahead five years — isn’t complicated and dense. The film opens in 1972, because that’s when Judy and eighty other activists staged a sit-in on Madison Avenue to protest the vetoing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which we’re told was one of the very first pieces of federal legislation meant to guarantee certain rights to people with disabilities (from accessibility to education). The act was eventually signed in 1973, but when the film picks back up in 1978, it has not been implemented. It needed one last step: a signature from newly-installed Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo). And he wasn’t signing.

Heder and Taussig’s script distills the legal wrangling down well: this piece of legislation will help bring about massive positive change for the disabled community, but it will cost a lot of money, and Califano has already been asked to slash the budget. These are excellent stakes.

Judy doesn’t care about the cost to the government — why should she? — but she does care about the cost to her community. A seasoned and dogged activist, most of the people in Judy’s life are disabled in some way, and it’s her mission to a) wrangle them into action and b) be pretty pushy about it. Heder and her casting directors Bernard Telsey and Adam Caldwell have assembled a wonderful, winning cast around Madeley (herself a wheelchair user), including a number of disabled performers, cast here as icons in their own right. Standouts include Madeline Delp as Kitty Cone (the honey to Judy’s vinegar), Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, Antwan Tolliver as Brad Lomax, “CODA” star Daniel Durant as Steve McCleeland, Roberta Colindrez as Joni Breves, and instant star Charlie Rush-Reese as Dennis Billups.

That Heder would cast actually disabled people in these roles should seem obvious (this is the filmmaker behind “CODA,” after all), but there’s no question that it totally pays off all the same. The wide array of performers on offer here is thrilling, and it’s a treat to see them all settling in so well to this period world, rendered tactile and realistic by smart costuming choices by Danny Glicker and unfussy production design by John P. Goldsmith.

Enraged over the lack of movement on the signing of 504, Judy and her compatriots launch a series of protests around the country, focused on federal buildings that house HEW offices. Califano, stuck back in DC, can only hear about these events as they unfold, utterly stymied but what to do, paralyzed by fear for his job, and intent on reminding people he’s one of the good guys (he supported the Selma marches!). But the world has changed. When Judy somewhat impulsively leads a pack of protesters inside the SF federal building, what follows will only spark further change.

Despite the historical implications that follow — the SF sit-in became one of the country’s largest — Heder doesn’t noodle on the cultural vegetable aspect of this story. Instead, “Being Heumann” becomes something unexpectedly frisky and fun. The sit-in comes with plenty of challenges (beyond the myriad needs of the disabled community, there’s in-fighting to spare, government pressures galore, and deep worries about how it might actually pan out), but there’s also a streak of joy that runs through it. It’s thrilling to see people doing literally whatever they can for their well-being, and having a good time in the process (yes, you’ll get acquainted with their “sex tents” soon enough). There are almost too many colorful characters here, a sprawling ensemble in which everyone deserves their own film, though we occasionally lose some threads along the way.

That isn’t always easy for Judy, though, who remains set in her ways even as she sees real change happening around her. Madeley captures the real Judy Heumann’s energy beautifully; she’s funny and flinty and spiky and smarter than anyone else around her and totally driven by her sense of justice and equality. But that’s not always enough, a lesson that “Being Heumann” is not shy about. Fighting for what’s right involves just that, fighting. Sometimes, that even means fighting your own instincts.

A film like ”Being Heumann” is destined to be called rousing — a call to action that’s every bit as entertaining as it is inspiring. It’s a film about tough choices and even tougher circumstances, but it’s also about the tangible good that can come from people working together. What could be more joyous than that? More biopics could learn from this formula, and from this feeling. Be more like Judy: be tough, but never be afraid of joy.

“Being Heumann” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

#3482. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Pumpkin Lights’ adds a fun jack-o-lantern to your Mac’s menu bar

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Pumpkin Lights is a nifty little menu bar app for Mac that lets you quickly toggle between light mode and dark mode with a ray-traced jack-o-lantern that drops down from the top of your screen. It’s completely free, and very fun to utilize.

If you remember the Festivas menu bar app from Mac year, Pumpkin Lights is very similar in concept.

Pumpkin Lights brings a jack-o-lantern to your menu bar, just in time for halloween. It’s a nice decoration, and there’s plenty of different ways to customize it. You can “grow” many different pumpkin designs, as well as pick between four different color variants.

When you click on the pumpkin or pull on it, your Mac will toggle between light and dark mode – at least by default. Pumpkin Lights also has the option to open an app/website, keep your Mac awake, mute a sound, run a command, or run a shortcut of your choice.

The jack-o-lantern does have proper physics, so you can actually toss it around a bit and move it around in a novel way. You can customize the rope it hangs from, and much more. There’s also an option to have a hanging light bulb that serves a similar purpose.

Why Pumpkin Lights? Here’s what the developer has to say:

The idea came from something most of us do every day without thinking: switching between Light and Dark Mode. It’s always a toggle buried in Control Center or System Settings, and it never feels like anything. I wanted it to feel like touching a real object. So instead of a flat icon, the pumpkin and the bulb are real 3D models, ray-traced in real time, hanging on cords you can swing and spin. When the candle lights, its glow comes through the carved face. I spent most of my time on small details like how the cords move and how light falls on the pumpkin, because I wanted it to still feel delightful the hundredth time you use it, not just the first.

Pumpkin Lights is a completely free utility. You can download it from the developer’s website here, and it’s available for any Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or later. You can also follow the developer on Twitter.

#3481. Chicago Fire’s 300th Episode Fasttracks Its Death By A Thousand Cuts | Review

NBC celebrates a rare milestone as Chicago Fire hits 300th episode. Unfortunately, the hour fails to be match the importance of the moment.

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Ana has also covered a wide-spread of topics in the past — from franchises like, the MCU and Star Wars, to classic TV favorites, such as Frasier and MASH.

Ana brings clarity and enthusiasm to every story she tackles—whether reporting on new releases or offering deep dives into fan-favorite franchises. Her coverage translates complex entertainment developments into engaging, audience-focused content.

For a milestone as rare as hitting 300 episodes, Chicago Fire fails to deliver a memorable celebratory episode. As NBC's fall 2026 slate continues to rely on fully-established projects led by the Law & Order franchise, One Chicago's inaugural series continues to build its own legacy as the third-longest-running procedural on the network. Premiering in 2012, Chicago Fire is arguably the most popular first-responder show on TV right now. Aside from paving the way for spinoffs, such as Chicago PD and Chicago Med, it also inspired a string of shows in the same sandbox, with both ABC and CBS trying to replicate its success.

After 14 years on the air, Chicago Fire celebrates its 300th episode with "Three Hundred." Considering the ongoing trend of TV seasons getting fewer and shorter, this feat is becoming increasingly rare, which is a reminder of the show's longevity. Throughout the last decade and a half of its run, Chicago Fire has had its fair share of celebratory episodes. 2016's "One Hundred," 2019's "The Plunge," 2021's "Two Hundred," and 2024's "Inside Man" all delivered bigger and more consequential narratives that either honored the show's past or set up its future. For "Three Hundred," the focus is on the latter, as the outing marks a major shift in Firehouse 51.

NBC and Wolf Entertainment use Chicago Fire season 15, episode 5, as the send-off for Joe Minoso's Joe Cruz — one of the very few cast members who have been in the series since season 1. Given that, there was an expectation that "Three Hundred" would deliver a highly-emotional swan song for the character, despite the fact that the project has been gradually building towards his exit ever since his paralysis narrative started. Unfortunately, the lack of focus, the sheer number of plots simultaneously happening, and other head scratchers result in an ultimate letdown.

As Cruz's final outing, there was an expectation going into the episode that the hour would put an effort into highlighting his legacy with Firehouse 51 while also laying out a justified reason for his departure. Over the years, Chicago Fire has seen its fair share of character exits, and while some are done better than others, NBC and Wolf Entertainment have done decently when it comes to sending off characters who were on the show for a considerable amount of time. Sadly, that isn't the case for Cruz. "Three Hundred" starts with the character doing considerably better, with Chicago Med's Dean Archer even telling him that he would be back at Firehouse 51 soon enough. Everyone is on board with the idea, except for Chloe, who gives birth to their twins early due to overall stress about doing everything for the family. Apparently, she had been against her husband going back to work, afraid that he would be hurt again and she would be left alone.

While it makes sense for her to be worried, the way Chicago Fire establishes this reveal is so poorly-executed. It makes Chloe look unreasonable, considering how much Cruz has been working hard to get back to work. On top of that, her husband giving up his career and means of living at this point in their family life seems impractical in terms of their economic standing. Now, Cruz doesn't have any path towards going back to work. The fact that this whole plot happens separate from anyone over at Firehouse 51 makes it worse. Firehouse 51 has always differentiated itself by being a tightly-knit team, and yet, it's odd that there's no effort to help Cruz's family beyond making sure that he can return to Squad 3 — even then, Kelly Severide's attempt to convince him to stay sounds self-serving.

Granted that it still has to move on beyond Cruz's stint with Firehouse 51, the least Chicago Fire could have done is give him a compelling and solid swan song, not something that makes it seem like an afterthought.

Instead of focusing on Cruz's struggle for a more emotional send-off, Chicago Fire season 15, episode 5 tackles several more stories separate from its main plot. Stella Kidd deals with a probationary struggling after a call, Christopher Herrmann has an odd arc regarding his new professional headshot, while Violet Mikami and Lyla Novak deal with personal stories. "Three Hundred" even opens with Severide working on an arson case. Granted that it still has to move on beyond Cruz's stint with Firehouse 51, the least Chicago Fire could have done is give him a compelling and solid swan song, not something that makes it seem like an afterthought. Even the poignant tribute to Otis Zvonecek at the end of the hour doesn't have the emotional impact that it should have.

To better understand the failures of Chicago Fire's 300th episode, it's important to remember that the outing doesn't exist in a bubble. It's a culmination of all the small but detrimental issues that the project has been facing in the last few years. Now, the pile has gotten so big that it's nearly impossible to ignore. For starters, Minoso's exit is primarily motivated by NBC's yearly cost-cutting measures. While some actors left on their own, a handful of them, especially in more recent years, were written out of Chicago Fire and One Chicago in general to cut costs. This has resulted in sudden story shifts, as the writers scramble to find a way to write out a character in the quickest way possible.

Secondly, and still tied to the first point, the constant changing of the ensemble makes it difficult for Chicago Fire to properly establish a new overall dynamic. On a smaller scale, one-on-one relationships are also scarce outside the long-standing ones, such as Herrmann and Randall "Mouch" McHolland's friendship, as well as Severide and Kidd's romance. These types of pairings were the backbone of the Chicago Fire during its earliest years, as effectively emphasized by the bittersweet moment between Cruz and Otis. Now, since no new character stays long enough, any kind of personal and relationship build-up goes out of the window.

One fan-favorite series on NBC will officially make tv history by breaking an industry record that has been established over two decades ago.

As Chicago Fire season 15 continues, hopefully, it is able to find the balance that it needs to be able to sustain another 300-episode run. The show has one of the most engaged fan communities, and it would be a shame if these problems continue to plague it until it's eventually canceled.

#3480. The 6 Worst Steamy Thriller Movies of All Time, Ranked

A New York native, Joe graduated from an avant-garde theater school upstate, where he was obsessed with sketch comedy. There, he and his lunatic friends founded The Sketchies — which still lives on at Skidmore College today. Living in New York City, a screenwriter friend of his then taught him how to write for film. This awakened a new passion in Joe. Since then his scripts have garnered over 200 festival selections, nominations, and wins all over the globe (including the BlueCat Best Feature award). Several of his screenplays have been made into feature films — some of them not that bad! Overall, he loves to create unique, hilarious, touching, and bizarre stories.

The steamy thriller had its hot and heavy heyday through the 80s and early 90s, with sultry hits like Body Heat, Fatal Attraction, and Basic Instinct. A few modern takes on this sub-genre succeeded in more recent years as well, like Fifty Shades of Grey, Love, and The Handmaiden. However, as with any trend pervasive in the film world, countless imitators of these sensually stimulating, smoldering flicks have emerged, with limited success (for instance, the 50 Shades sequels…).

Here are the absolute worst steamy romance-thrillers ever made, all proudly produced with little to no redeeming qualities. Some of these films focus on what the filmmakers hoped would be a thrilling plot line imbued with arousing scenes of unbridled bliss — while others opted to forgo any attempt at a compelling story and simply showcased extended sequences of gratuitous carnal desires. No matter how they tried to captivate viewers, all these movies failed in flagrant fashion, delivering far more hot air than steam.

While there are more “older woman has affair with younger guy that turns dangerous” movies in the Lifetime thriller catalog than there are fetching fish in the sea, at least those guilty pleasure Lifetime flicks aren’t trying to pass themselves off as real, intellectually stimulating films. The Jennifer Lopez vehicle, director Rob Cohen’s The Boy Next Door, is a laughably corny attempt at erotically-charged thrills that falls flat in pretty much every way conceivable.

Claire Peterson (Lopez) is a high school lit teacher, and a caring mom to her son, Kevin (Ian Nelson). She’s recently divorced from her cheating husband, Garrett Peterson (John Corbett), and, of course, is in a vulnerable state. When Noah Sandborn (Ryan Guzman), a muscular bad boy who boasts the tender age of 19, moves in next door (get it?), the viewer knows that sparks are about to fly. Yes, Claire jettisons her good judgment and gives in to her primal desire for a good romp. She and Noah share a night of passionate May-December romance. Claire comes to her senses and tries to end things there, but Noah ain’t havin’ it. He turns from charming neighbor to deranged stalker almost overnight. The spurned Noah wants to wreck Claire’s life now, and the movie culminates in a ridiculous sequence involving a barn inferno and the classic trope of Chekov’s EpiPen. With a 12% RT score, this movie is borderline dumb, straining credulity at every turn.

Madonna is a tremendous entertainer, that is not in question. Now, her acting ability? Well, in all fairness, she’s had some moments — comedy seems more up her alley than drama, as evidenced by a decent lead performance in Desperately Seeking Susan. However, her bold attempt at a steamy thriller, is a massive fail. Yet, it absolutely must be noted, the blame doesn’t solely rest on Madge’s shoulders. The direction by Uli Edel is borderline at best, the editing feels rushed, and the worst offender may just be the screenwriter, Brad Mirman. This script feels like it was made with A.I. before A.I. was even a thing (using the keywords: cocaine, Madonna, sex, and “fall out window”).

The story initially does hold water. Rebecca Carlson (Madonna) is an alluring woman who becomes involved with a crusty older dude, Andrew Marsh (Michael Forest). As one may ingeniously predict, her heart isn’t exactly pure, and she’s apparently out for his crusty old loot. Rebecca uses her body as a weapon, and basically sexes the feeble-hearted Andrew to death (the ticker can only take so much BDSM fun). Rebecca doesn’t get off Scott-free, and so she desperately needs the help of her lawyer, Frank Dulaney (Willem Dafoe), to help exonerate her. So, voilà, she sleeps with him. But, just when the viewer thinks they have Rebecca's motivations all figured out, a wild twist is introduced. The problem is, this twist is dumb as dirt, and the film’s finale is immensely unsatisfying — resulting in an 8% RT score.

Director Zalman King was really hoping he could cash in on the buzz of his beloved steamy thriller 9½ Weeks, by casting the then hottie Mickey Rourke again and sticking him into another lust-filled story. Alas, he failed — only now, internationally. Wild Orchid is set in Rio, Brazil, a city with the reputation of being quite a hot place, in all definitions of the word. Unfortunately, this histrionic take on the mismatched love story is a cinematic abomination with a 10% critic score on RT.

Soft-spoken real estate lawyer, Emily Reed (supermodel Carré Otis), has to take a trip to Rio to close a big hotel acquisition deal for her client, along with her co-worker, Claudia Dennis (Jacqueline Bisset). While chilling in the “Cidade Maravilhosa,” Emily encounters a wealthy American, James Wheeler (Rourke). Naturally, James knows all the hot, sexy spots in town, and ushers Emily on a verboten, erotic journey of self-discovery. The self-assured sexual puppet master that is James is eventually revealed to have once been a destitute orphan with a stutter — who grew up to be the callous, handsome money-maker he is today. Through their shared experiences in carnal Carnival intimacy, James finally sheds his hard exterior, and he and Emily find true love. Ok, sure. Unlike 9½ Weeks, Wild Orchid doesn’t have much of a story going for it, and has been mostly viewed as an onion paper-thin excuse for mostly unnecessary, silly soft-core action.

Some steamy thrillers are so widely adored that they inspire a sequel. Such is the case with the dismal cinematic detritus that is Basic Instinct 2. Director Michael Caton-Jones and fellow filmmakers surely believed that Sharon Stone’s Catherine Tramell character would be captivating enough to draw audiences in droves. They. Were. Wrong.

The tale sees Catherine relocate to London to start fresh. Right off the bat, she gets into a drug-fueled car wreck that takes the life of a famous footballer, Kevin Franks (Stan Collymore). The court system in England seems just as favorable to Catherine as that of its U.S. counterpart, and Catherine just has to receive treatment for her “danger addict” lifestyle from a forensic psychiatrist, Dr. Michael Glass (David Morrissey). As Catherine slinks her way into his bed, and blows up his personal and professional life in the process, a bunch of adjacent bodies begin to pile up. Without spoiling the “twist” ending too much, it seems that Catherine has once again used her wiles to compel men to do very bad things for her… With a 6% score on RT (hey, at least it’s not zero), this soggy sequel is a mostly flat, wannabe provocative work of forced drudgery.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

This colorful movie almost doesn’t make this list as it is precipitously close to being a “so bad it’s good” flick…yet, alas, here it is. There are so many confounding things about this movie, really from start to finish (for instance, a car that's blindly sent flying off a building’s roof to try to squish the protagonist), but none may be as convoluted and flat-out baffling as the film’s grand finale of nonsensical, endless twists. Indeed, director Richard Rush’s Color of Night is one long sex scene punctuated with one ludicrous plot point after the next.

The gloriously bizarre plot follows a troubled psychiatrist, Dr. Bill Capa (Bruce Willis, with a rare miss), who, after witnessing one of his patients take their own life, suddenly goes color-blind. He catches a flight across the country to L.A., to hang with his fellow headshrinker bud, Dr. Bob Moore (Scott Bakula). However, Bobby is soon murdered, and the prime suspect is one of his group therapy patients. There is a host of hilariously diverse personalities here, and Dr. Bill opts to take over the group sessions while he’s there. Most notably, there is a troubled boy named “Richie” in the group. Now, a nubile young woman, Rose (Jane March), shows up at Bob’s house and soon “befriends” Bill. Also, she has a romantic relationship with another member of the group, Sondra (Lesley Ann Warren). In any event, Bill has wildly graphic pool intercourse with Rose, and then shower sex, and so on. Finally, (spoiler here, but really, who cares) the film concludes with the big reveal that Rose is also Richie, as she has multiple personality disorder…and is also being controlled by her maniacally manipulative brother, Dale Dexter (Andrew Lowery), forced to be complicit in committing murders…for some reason. It’s all so confusing and melodramatically laid out, that it begs credibility and strains logic at every turn. Naturally, Rose goes to the roof to fling herself off, but after a struggle, Bill saves her. And gets his color sight back. Sure, why not.

Oof. As the title implies, this Blanka Lipińska-penned novel turned Netflix movie covers a year of tortuous action. The issue is that it’s more painful for the audience to endure than the main character. Predicated on the ancient idea that “kidnapping can be sexy,” co-writer/directors Barbara Bialowas and Tomasz Mandes’s exploration of forced “love” is what the kiddos today would call the epitome of cringe.

The story follows a wealthy, striking mafia man, Massimo Torricelli (Michele Morrone), who becomes enraptured with a gorgeous, astute and savvy businesswoman, Laura Biel (Anna-Maria Sieklucka). Instead of talking to her, Massimo takes the only logical course of action: kidnap her and compel her to fall madly in love with him. He has a year to convince her that they are soul mates, and if he fails, he’ll let her go (wow, what a gentleman). Laura initially rebuffs his advances, but through a series of manipulative moves enacted by Massimo, Laura eventually succumbs to Stockholm Syndrome and has passionate sex with the Italian stallion. Critics didn’t love the premise or execution, and 365 Days received a 0% Tomatometer score on RT. Audiences were a bit more forgiving, with the film garnering a 36% Popcornmeter rank. The directors at least knew how to exploit the beautiful backdrops of Warsaw and Sicily, along with their leads’ physiques, but make no mistake, this is an offensively bad movie, in every sense. Widely panned for its overtly anti-feminist themes and machismo-centric motifs, this clunker seemed to undo decades of progress. Yet, somehow, Netflix granted it not one, but two sequels, completing a trilogy in true terribleness.

#3479. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3478. Here’s how the new MacBook Pro and macOS 27 are optimized for touch

Apple just unveiled the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, its first MacBook with a touch display. While Apple already added a handful of touch optimizations to macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this year, there’s also a number of new optimizations that were unveiled alongside the new MacBook Pro. Here’s what Apple worked on.

With the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the traffic light icons in the top left of an app window will get bigger when you’re tapping them, making the touch targets a little bit larger.

Gestures that you can normally perform on the trackpad can also be performed on the screen. Whether that be a three-finger swipe up for mission control, three-finger swipes to switch spaces, pinching to zoom, or scrolling on a web page. You can also access Spotlight from the Dynamic Island, similar to how iPhones handle it on iOS 27.

If you’re an app developer, you’ll really appreciate this change: with the new MacBook Pro, you can fully navigate the iOS simulator with touch. No need to try to replicate touch gestures on a trackpad.

When you interact with a context menu in the menu bar, each of the items within a menu will get a little bit larger for touch. Additionally, most optimized apps will have larger touch targets, even if the buttons don’t necessarily appear bigger.

All in all, there’s a handful of optimizations already in macOS 27 Golden Gate for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. On top of what was named here, Apple also added pull to refresh in Safari and slightly larger spacing between menu bar items to all Macs with macOS 27.

Yeeeeeeeah no. Interactions with any of the onscreen elements are incredibly tedious, sporadic, and glitchy. This isn’t the company Steve Jobs started, it’s just Microsoft with an Apple logo.

Apple also says there’s more to come on the Mac when it comes to touch optimizations, so we’ll likely see much more in store at the next WWDC.

What do you think about touch support on the new MacBook Pro? Are you looking forward to it eventually trickling down to every Mac? Let us know in the comments.

#3477. ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Ask any gay man with a social media account, and they likely have an opinion about Jordan Firstman. The backlash-courting queer actor/comedian, controversial most recently because of an online flare-up over querying the sexual realism of “Heated Rivalry,” is labeled either candid or confrontational. He also has a record of taking on sexually explicit projects like Sebastian Silva’s suicide-ideating, ketamine-fueled dark comedy “Rotting in the Sun.” His status as a self-aware, hyper-online provocateur may not seem to suggest the makings of a bona fide filmmaker, but just wait. Related Stories ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

While that reputation might have Firstman on guard as he debuts his feature writing/directing debut “Club Kid,” as it will certain circumspect corners of the audience, this terrific movie should put any of those nervous feelings to rest. Even his haters won’t be able to resist what’s announced here as a major filmmaking talent with a sensitive side that belies his brash, internet-based persona.

He also stars as the protagonist of his hugely crowd-pleasing, excruciatingly funny, and poignant first film — one that plays to all sides of the room despite being brazenly, unapologetically queer — which will prime Firstman-savvy viewers to immediately interpret “Club Kid” as autobiographical. That’s because it is.

He plays party promoter Peter, now in his thirties after a decade-plus of MDMA-addled revelry, the kind where all the days blur and blot into one long and sweaty night with a coming horizon in the shape of regret. Firstman may not be playing himself this time, but he is playing a version of that self, having, as he says, spent enough years in Berlin to be labeled “the angel of Berghain” by his new friends, but now ready to put the days-that-became-years of GHB, MDMA, and other letters of the alphabet behind him.

“Club Kid” is exactly about what happens when the lights go up on the party, the shameover of the morning after that becomes a way of being, and the need to do it all over again to stave off last night’s aching after effects. But it’s also about — earnesty alert! — family lost and found, not only because of the queer community formed around the now-orphaned Peter, who lives in the rent-controlled Manhattan his mother left him after she died, but because he wakes up one day to find a child he fathered and never knew about, literally on his doorstep.

“Club Kid” was shot on 35mm on location in New York City with a team of backers including “Anora” Oscar-winning producer Alex Coco and nepo filmmaker Olmo Schnabel, and a millennial cast of queer comedians. So it’s hard not to leave the movie thinking all that’s needed here is an A24 logo slapped onto the opening credits, and it’s ready for the world. But no matter; while Firstman’s aesthetic is loudly in A24’s register, it turns out to be an asset rather than a limitation.

Beginning inside a sensually lit, drug-soaked party and ending as one rages on without you from afar, “Club Kid” drops us into Brooklyn 2016. Peter, sing-screaming Rihanna’s “Sex with Me” in a clown car of an Uber ride with his friends, is headed into yet another bender to remember (but also eventually forget). At a club of the sort that now dominates night culture in Bushwick, rising party promoter Peter ends up hooking up — and then really hooking up — with a couple of hyperactive “innit, babes?” British women in the back room. It’s all inconspicuously taking a turn for the sexual when the movie smash cuts to “a decade or so later,” when the proverbial party is still dying down, but Peter is still living in it — albeit more sweaty and tragic 10 years on.

He’s now made a career out of his drug use with his best friend and business partner Sophie (a marvelous, perpetually coked-out Cara Delevingne, who’s two inches from a breakdown at all times). A few days before the one that’s about to change his life, they have an important sit-down coming up with FiDi investors to help expand their New York party empire. But alas, as he couldn’t help himself once again the night before, Peter wakes up drugged to the gills, rushing to the meeting only to nod off at the table, still in a GHB-spiked stupor. (His reaction to a dropper of hot sauce that looks curiously similar to the one he used last night to get high is one of the film’s many brilliantly funny little pratfalls.)

All of that’s to say Peter’s life is still totally a mess, and his arrested development from a decade of partying has now washed him out to the point where sobriety is maybe never part of his day. (A weekend spent dissipated, hungover, jerking off to internet porn and eating Popeye’s in bed rings painfully true.)

Party’s certainly over, though, when one of those British “innit babes” from 10 years ago, Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), shows up from London at his apartment (where Peter lives with an “Azerbaijanian aspiring queer philosopher” who doesn’t pay rent) with an eight-year-old boy. “You’ve got a kid! ‘Yay!,’” she tells him while delivering the news that Arlo (preternaturally gifted young breakout actor Reggie Absalom) is in fact Peter’s child with one of the other women from that opening-scene heterosexual encounter, who’s just died. The first and only time Peter fucked a woman, and now he’s fucked himself into having to finish raising a small boy.

Cue the manic panic, more drug use, and resignation to the idea that there’s no sending this kid back to the U.K.

While it’s a bit sudden how fast the switch flips from Peter feeling wildly ill-equipped for parenting to becoming a nurturing caretaker, he and Arlo turn out to have more in common than not. Arlo, for one, has the music taste of someone who grew up on Pitchfork, eagerly taking to the $300 Elliott Smith record Peter buys for him in a later scene. (The soundtrack on this thing, by the way, rules, from Arthur Russell during the film’s melancholy final act to “The White Lotus” composer Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s deeply felt original score.) Their relationship, however quickly, becomes the film’s so-far unexpected sweet center, as Peter starts to really appreciate and eventually love Arlo, who has traumas of his own.

A lot of the success of “Club Kid” rides not only on Firstman’s shoulders, but also on the collaborators he’s working with, including cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra who captures a certain lost-era grit in New York as well as in the chaos-packed nightclub sequences. “Club Kid” also takes advantage of New York City as not just a backdrop but a central character in the storytelling, using the city in a way that feels rare onscreen these days.

“Club Kid” freewheels and unwinds like a head rush of a zippy party movie until Arlo’s introduction brings the comedown. It turns out he feels more at home among Peter’s “found family” of queer revelers, discovering his own DJ skills in the process, than he ever did in London. Could Peter really warm to fatherhood? Real emotional stakes start to heighten as he begins recognizing the unexpected realities of his new arrangement, like getting Arlo into school, or keeping the boy shielded from the drug use of his friends while Peter’s own finally starts to diminish. A nervous, tentative romance comes into view with child psychologist Oscar (Diego Calva), and on a date where a namecheck of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin” becomes not just a tender confession, but a turn-on.

“Club Kid” takes a sharp dramatic turn, in which the nature of Arlo’s living situation becomes even more dire and probably illegal, that almost shouldn’t work in a comedy like this — but it’s a turn that feels inevitable given how “Club Kid” is structured like the rise and fall of a drug experience, a high that crashes down into despair. The emotional arc bends toward “Kramer vs. Kramer” territory with a cathartic (and well-played by Firstman) courtroom oner. Peter may be insecure about his own place in a world where only parts of it have room for him, but as a storyteller with an eye, Firstman is anything but.

Firstman is by now an established comedic voice, but his work on all sides of the camera here leaves pretty of room for revelation, for him to become a genuine discovery beyond an audience of gay, internet-addled millennials. “Club Kid” has real potential to break out bigger than its seemingly niche scope would suggest, with Firstman finally shirking the ironic pose he’s taken online for years to emerge as a sincere storyteller with heart as much as humor.

“Club Kid” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3476. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3474. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3473. ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Many scenes in “Wildwood” are designed to look spectacular. Even if each frame weren’t already rendered with the meticulous detail and artistry of stop-motion animation, the Laika Studios film is full of complex, chaotic battle sequences, a forest writhing with eldritch magic, and giant eagles soaring through the sky.

But some of the most technically challenging scenes, according to director Travis Knight, aren’t the ones that look the most majestic. They are — true to the spirit of the film and the lesson learned by its stubborn, caring protagonist Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) — the simple magic of everyday life. Related Stories ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

In fact, Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast that one of the most challenging sequences in “Wildwood” was simply getting its hero from one end of her bedroom to the other. Laika prefers Canon cameras mounted on large motion-control rigs, which offer the flexibility needed to capture puppet movements adjusted one frame at a time. But when the camera moves, it also has to do so one painstaking frame at a time.

Knight, who’s now directed live-action features “Bumblebee” and “Masters of the Universe” in addition to his Laika work on “Kubo and the Two Strings,” wanted “Wildwood” to have the same camera language as a live-action film. He wanted the intimacy and wordless visual storytelling of a camera tracking Prue as she huffs across her bedroom, where the camera movement helps us see the decor shift from the artifacts of a carefree kid to those of a more disaffected teen.

“I still wanted it to feel like it was shot like a live-action film, with that kind of intimacy with the camera. But a camera on a motion-control rig is the size of a Ford F-150 in our [puppet-scale] world. It’s huge. And so if a camera is moving, you have to create space for the camera on set,” Knight said.

This is on top of creating space for the animator, who is roughly the size of a Kaiju in comparison to the fifth-scale the humans on either side of the Impassable Wood live at. The Prue puppet is roughly 10 inches tall. Being able to move that puppet and a camera at least as large as her bedroom that the puppet is moving through? That is a particularly gnarly feat of physics.

“We essentially had to deconstruct the set,” Knight said. “It was almost like it was a clamshell. It would open to make room for the camera, and then it would close up again. It was such a complicated engineering feat, when all it is [for] is a camera panning across a room. Those are the kinds of challenges that the team has to figure out, which is stupid, but it’s what it requires if you’re trying to tell a story like this.”

There is much to be said, and rightly, about the awe-inducing moments of spectacle in “Wildwood.” The Laika team had to figure out how to make giant puppets out of fabric and feathers instead of standard-issue silicone to simulate flight compellingly, accurately, and tactilely. Combat sequences required enormous attention to detail. But when Knight watches the film, he’s just as struck by the invisible work that makes “Wildwood” feel like a live-action epic — the thankless but involving work that viewers aren’t ever meant to see.

“I learned a great many things about what to do, what not to do [working in live-action]. It fundamentally changed my relationship with the camera, which is one of the reasons why ‘Wildwood’ looks so different. It’s because I wanted it to feel as if it were without the inherent limitations you would typically find in stop-motion cinematography,” Knight said. “When I see this movie, I am seeing all these little miraculous moments of engineering and artistry and human creativity at play on the big screen, and that’s one of the reasons it moves me so much.”

#3472. Every Robin in Order From The First Boy Wonder to DC’s New Heir, Explained

The caped crusader patrolling Gotham by night may always cast a massive shadow over Batman's fellow defenders, but that hasn't made the Robins of the DC Universe any less significant. In fact, many have splintered to chart impressive paths of their own, forging key bonds and iconic teams.

Naturally, every reader, viewer, or general consumer of DC media will encounter an instance in which they learn just how many Robins there are. In certain limited instances, untold legions of those bearing the title have existed either in reality or in detailed visions of an alternate future. But many have indeed lived as the primary character bearing the Robin title as Batman's sidekick, and more than one has even died doing the same.

Robins throughout DC continuity have emerged from all walks of life, shouldering trauma, obsession, or general issues of their own. They're often the product of their era, with their fates occasionally decided by committee, in the case of Jason Todd. But every named Robin deserves the spotlight if even briefly, to showcase how far each of them have come.

Robin, Nightwing, Batman, Agent 37, Renegade, Talon, Deadman, Ric Grayson

Like Bruce Wayne, Dick witnessed his parents' murder. Feeling a kinship with the boy, Bruce took him in as his ward and eventually trained him as his crime-fighting partner. After his tenure as Robin, Dick assumed the identity of Nightwing, carving out his path as a hero independent of Batman.

Since then, he has taken on diverse roles, such as a super spy, police officer, and leader of the Titans. Notably, he even filled in as Batman, with Bruce's son Damian serving as his Robin, during a time when Bruce was believed to be dead. There have been plenty of variants on Dick across decades of comics, with cases like Earth 2 where he functioned both as an attorney and as Robin well into adulthood, affiliated with the JSA of his world, too. Despite his many later identities, Dick is easily still the most iconic Robin, a label he'll never fully leave behind.

According to Detective Comics #226, Bruce Wayne was the original Robin, though this was later retconned in Post-Crisis canon. Before this change, Bruce trained under Detective Harvey Harris, who taught him the basics of detective work in the guise of the future Robin identity.

What’s particularly intriguing is that despite not knowing Dick Grayson, Bruce still adopted the classic Boy Wonder costume in the exact form it would later take. It was also Harris who coined the sidekick's nickname, noting Bruce's skills: "Since you're brilliant as a robin redbreast in that costume, I'll call you-- Robin!"

In one of the least known chapters of Robin's history in DC Comics, Bruce Wayne didn't just see the Robin uniform worn by another teen after Dick Grayson, but actually adopted another "son" named Lance Bruner. An orphan, entrusted to Bruce after his parents' death.

Lance was basically the opposite of Dick Grayson, competing with his new brother through deceit, manipulation, and outright lying to Bruce. So when Lance's snooping revealed they were acting as Batman and Robin, he took his opportunity to sell both of them out to Gotham's gangsters for his own payday

Thankfully, in the end, Lance's conscience got the better of him, and he arrived on the scene just in time to witness the death of Robin (or so he thought). Believing Dick dead, Lance donned the same Robin costume and took a bullet intended for Batman. It cost Lance his life, and a legacy as the second Robin... which everyone soon forgot about.

Robin, Red Hood, Red Robin, Batman, Wingman, Arkham Knight

Jason Todd assumed the role of Robin following Dick's departure. However, his tenure as Robin was marked by controversy, and DC Comics famously conducted a poll allowing fans to determine if he'd live or die in the A Death in the Family storyline.

Unsurprisingly, the majority of fans voted for his demise, leading to Jason's death at the hands of the Joker. However, that wasn’t the end of Jason Todd, who eventually came back to life via unknown forces. After a dip in a Lazarus pool and training with the League of Assassins, Jason took up the Red Hood mantle.

Batman: The Dark Knight Returns #1 (June 1986)

Chronologically, Carrie Kelley was the third character to adopt the Robin mantle. However, she exists outside mainstream continuity, residing solely within Frank Miller’s alternate universe of The Dark Knight Returns (1986). Kelley made her debut as half of the Dynamic Duo after an aged Batman, fresh out of retirement, rescued her from would-be muggers.

Inspired by his heroics, she acquired a Robin costume and armed herself with a slingshot loaded with firecrackers, thrusting herself into the Dark Knight’s world. Kelley notably played a pivotal role in defeating the resurfaced Joker and later assumed the mantles of Catgirl, Batgirl, and Batwoman.

Tim Drake inserted himself into Batman’s life, assuming the Robin mantle to assist a grieving Bruce, who was becoming increasingly violent after Jason’s death; recognizing that Batman NEEDED a Robin to function properly.

Tim is renowned as the boy genius within the DC Universe, earning accolades from Batman himself, who acknowledged Tim's exceptional intellect, possibly surpassing his own. He has earned the respect of adversaries like Ra’s al Ghul, who dubbed him "Detective," a title previously reserved solely for Bruce. Tim took up the Red Robin mantle after Robin was given to Damian by Dick.

Initially known as the vigilante Spoiler, Stephanie Brown made waves in the Batman universe when she briefly assumed the mantle of Robin, becoming the first female Robin in Gotham's history. However, her tenure as Robin was short-lived and came to an end when she was nearly killed by Black Mask.

Matt Reeves' returning Batman series sets up the debut of its first Robin, and it will be one of the most iconic bearers of the DC mantle.

Surviving the ordeal, Stephanie's death was faked by Doctor Leslie Thompkins in an attempt to get the girl away from Bruce and his child-endangering crusade. Stephanie eventually returned to Gotham, where she later transitioned into the role of Batgirl, taking on a new identity while continuing her crusade against injustice.

Robin, RedBird, Batman, Nightwing, Damian al Ghul

Damian Wayne, the son of Bruce Wayne and supervillain Talia al Ghul, was raised as a child assassin by his mother before becoming the fifth child to take up the Robin mantle. What sets Damian’s Robin journey apart from others is that he was the Robin to Dick Grayson’s Batman, since Bruce was believed to be dead at the time.

As of 2024, Damian is currently Robin and is partnered with his father. Like Jason Todd, Damian also died while serving as Robin and was later brought back to life; upon his resurrection, Damian possessed surprising superpowers for a short time.

Despite varying fandom opinions, Duke did receive an official Robin badge of honor during the We Are Robin storyline. Following an altercation that leaves Duke unconscious, he wakes up believing he's in police custody and is asked what he's willing to do to locate his parents, to which he replies that it's the duty of the police.

Upon leaving the "interrogation," Duke stumbles upon a biker jacket with a yellow R, a cellphone in the pocket, and a motorcycle, signaling his status as a Robin. Duke's eventual inclusion in the Bat-Family further cements his legitimacy as a true Robin. But he'd carve an exciting new path for himself beyond that, too, with new adventures as the Signal to this day.

Duke, along with the previous four most significant Robin title-bearers, was recently featured in Absolute Batman's "Robin Program" assembled by the Joker to fight Batman. They're a heavily-armed, mechanized force with high mobility thanks to mech suits, motorcycles, and more, led by Captain Dick Grayson and overseen by General Slade Wilson. It quickly led to a dark direction with them already losing one in the heat of battle, and Bruce has hardly seen the last of them.

In 2014's Gotham Academy #1, Mia "Maps" Mizoguchi debuted and quickly became known among fans as an honorary Robin. Her deep admiration for Batman led her to adopt the red, yellow, and green of Robin, and she even collaborated with Batman on a case.

Despite never being officially inducted as a Girl Wonder, Maps has won over fans, particularly through her close friendship with Damian Wayne, Batman’s current Robin. Despite her unofficial status, Maps embodies the spirit, detective skills, and intelligence that make her a strong candidate for DC to fully integrate into the Bat-Family in the future.

I have tested and used countless charging stations over the years, and while many of them get the job done, I feel like there is always some sort of compromise. Whether it’s not enough power, lack of a certain port that I need, or slow wireless charging, I have yet to find one that truly checks every box for me. But over the last month, I have been using CUKTECH’s new 140W Powerstation, and it has nailed everything. It is a six-in-one desktop charger with a built-in retractable cable, magnetic wireless charging, and a dedicated diagnostic display, all in an aesthetic, compact package. Here is everything you need to know and why I think it’s worth considering.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video to see this CUKTECH 15 PowerStation in action!

At its core, the CUKTECH 15 PowerStation is a 140W GaN charger. It can charge one device at the full 140W, meaning it can charge your 16-in MacBook Pro PROLED XDR at max speed, or it can divvy up that power to charge up to six devices at once. It also offers a great combination of ports, a built-in cable, and multiple wireless charging options. You get:

Of course, the biggest selling point is the versatility of it all. You can charge your MacBook Pro with the main USB-C port, charge your iPad with the built-in cable, place your iPhone on the MagSafe charger, and place your AirPods on the wireless charging pad. After all of that, there are still more ports for other accessories that I use daily.

Do keep in mind that the 140W output is the total output, so if more devices are added, that output is shared across all the connected devices.

I am someone who is constantly switching between so many Apple devices. I switch between my iPad Pro and MacBook Pro all the time, and now that it is techtember, I am testing multiple iPhones at the same time, so I need to make sure all of my devices are charged up for when I need them. Not only that, but I also need a USB-A port for my camera battery charging station. So having a centralized hub to charge all of my devices is a MUST in my desk setup. So what immediately stands out to me about the CUKTECH 15 is how much functionality they were able to pack into this relatively compact charging station.

I am a huge fan of built-in retractable cables; they eliminate the need to remember to carry a USB-C cable, so you know you can charge at least one device. Then you add in the wireless magnetic charging stand that supports the new iPhone Duo and StandBy Mode, all while keeping the iPhone upright and visible. Also, when you set up that magnetic charging pad in the upright position, it reveals an AirPods Pro charger. The design is so well thought out.

The cherry on top of it all is the display. I love being able to see how fast something is charging. It allows me to see whether products meet their charging speed standards and how different devices are affected by their charge levels. CUKTECH was also smart to still include one USB-A port. Lots of companies have decided to omit that port because it is an old standard, but there are still plenty of older and wacky tech that uses USB-A, so the inclusion is appreciated. The only thing missing is a dedicated Apple Watch charger, but I just plug in my own when I need it.

The CUKTECH 15 140W Charging Station is available today on Amazon for $149. It has been out in Europe for a little while, but now it has finally made it to the US!

There are plenty of charging stations on the market, but CUKTECH’s 140W power station is the first to check off all the boxes for me. It’s compact, looks great, has all the ports and charging methods I need, and features a beautiful TFT display that lets me know things are charging as they should. If you use multiple devices throughout the day and need them charged at all times, this is worth considering.

#3470. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.
