Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3444. 110-Episode Space Opera Is A Masterclass In Sci-Fi Storytelling

Most sci-fi shows set in space look up and speculate about our place in the stars. However, one iconic space opera looks inward and explores our civilizations and geopolitical conflicts through its expansive galactic lens. Owing to this, the show in question still feels timeless even though it first premiered a long time ago.

Created by J. Michael Straczynski (JMS), Babylon 5 was meant to be a television novel. Each episode in the series was treated as a detailed chapter that perfectly tied into a larger pre-planned narrative. Even before the inception of its production, Babylon 5 was planned to have a 5-year arc with five whole seasons.

Unfortunately, as fate would have it, Babylon 5 faced the threat of cancellation after four seasons. Although its fifth and final season still saw the light of day, the cancellation threat slightly marred its narrative momentum. Still, after all these decades, Babylon 5 remains a masterclass in sci-fi storytelling, and more 21st century sci-fi TV shows should learn from its approach.

Episodic TV reigned supreme back in the 1990s. Some of the most popular '90s sci-fi shows, like Star Trek: The Next Generation, walked through fresh arcs in almost every episode to ensure viewers could walk in and out whenever they wanted. J. Michael Straczynski, however, hoped to get a little more ambitious than conventional additions to the genre.

He envisioned a grand space opera, Babylon 5, which had a pre-planned 5-year arc. JMS himself wrote 92 of Babylon 5's 110 episodes, ensuring that even the smallest details in the series had compelling payoffs much later. Apart from merely planning a long-term story for the series, Straczynski even accounted for production hiccups in his writing.

Realizing that some actors would not be able to commit to his long-term plans for the show, he intentionally set up narrative "trap doors." Each trap door ensured that an alternative story could emerge if a primary cast member from the series was forced to depart.

With this narrative setup, Babylon 5 maintained strong momentum even when Michael O'Hare (who played Sinclair) had to exit the show. Instead of completely breaking his storyline, JMS' established "trap door" evolved Sinclair's existing arc into a brilliant time loop twist.

Apart from its writing format, Babylon 5 was also known for its geopolitical realism. In its portrayal of space diplomacy, Babylon 5 features no black-and-white heroes or villains. Even some of the darkest characters in Babylon 5, like G'Kar, become incredibly rootable figures, while comical diplomats, like Londo, become victims of fascist ruin.

In its 110-episode runtime, the space opera also does an incredible job of building a fantastical world that feels both real and incredibly human. It features everything from unique alien species to distinct otherworldly religions and spiritual beliefs. Yet, its drama operates on a deeply human level where it highlights how prejudice and economic strain can never cease to exist.

The only aspect of the series that has not aged too well is its CGI. It was visually ahead of its time, but 30 years are enough to make a sci-fi series look dated. Owing to this, it is hard not to see how Babylon 5 is one space opera sci-fi that could really benefit from a reboot. Its reboot, however, will only work if it primarily focuses on improving the original show's visuals while still following JMS' original story plan.

Babylon 5 is a science fiction television series set on a space station built by the Earth Alliance. Released in 1994, it acts as a diplomatic sanctuary to preserve peace among various alien races, doubling as a military post and a bustling hub for travelers and traders. As Commander Jeffrey Sinclair and later Captain John Sheridan oversee the station, they become caught in a growing conspiracy and an ancient conflict that threatens the future of the galaxy

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

#3441. 5 Sci-Fi Books You Can Finish in a Weekend

Sci-fi can be a lot to take in, and that's understandable. Luckily, some of the best sci-fi books can be finished in two days or less. From time travel and alternate universes to human-made dystopias, the genre explores familiar and unfamiliar concepts, imagining worlds where technology seems to have no bounds and human intelligence has reached unimaginable heights.

But progress comes with consequences, no matter how logical a decision might seem. Science cannot exist without the humans who practice it, and ultimately, their morals determine whether it is used for good or bad. That's some pretty heavy philosophical stuff, but certain writers know how to tackle these ideas in shorter books or through plots that are a breeze to read. From an absurdly ridiculous take on alien encounters to a survival thriller set on Mars, here are sci-fi books you can finish in a weekend.

Winner of the 2020 Hugo Award for Best Novella, Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone's This Is How You Lose the Time War follows Blue and Red, two rival agents working for opposing organizations across different timelines and universes in a post-apocalyptic future. Both women are tasked with manipulating events in the past to secure the future their respective factions desire. Although they've crossed paths countless times during their missions, they've never exchanged a word — that is, until Blue breaks the routine (and the rules) by sending Red a letter. What begins as a simple exchange soon blossoms into a companionship that puts their reputations, loyalties, and duties at risk.

At approximately 200 pages, This Is How You Lose the Time War is told in an epistolary format, which makes sense given that Blue and Red's main form of communication is through letters. This also makes the novel an easily digestible read that you can finish in two days. However, its shorter length doesn't take away from the ambitious scope of the story, especially when concepts like branching timelines and alternate universes are often reserved for longer novels with extensive worldbuilding. But this novel is more than just sci-fi. It's also about a forbidden love with consequences that extend beyond the two people involved. Their relationship could potentially threaten the fragile nature of the universes themselves, showing how something as personal as love can have far-reaching scientific implications that put humanity at risk.

At around 200 pages, Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy stuffs an entire universe of ridiculous adventures into a surprisingly quick read. It all starts when Earth is demolished by the Vogons to make room for a hyperspace bypass, leaving ordinary Englishman Arthur Dent scrambling to survive. He escapes with Ford Prefect, an alien friend who takes him across the galaxy alongside a bizarre group of companions: the two-headed president Zaphod Beeblebrox, the chronically depressed robot Marvin, and Trillian, another human survivor. Their journey eventually brings Arthur closer to discovering Earth's actual purpose, which, naturally, involves a supercomputer.

Adams wastes little time making it clear that this isn't your typical sci-fi adventure. The universe operates on its own ridiculous logic, whether that means destroying an entire planet for a space shortcut or electing a two-headed president. The jokes come so frequently that readers barely have time to question the absurdity before the next one arrives. Beneath all that humor, the novel also takes a swipe at humanity's obsession with finding meaning in everything. People spend their lives searching for the ultimate answer to existence, only for the universe to offer very little in return. And when the supercomputer finally delivers its answer, the result is so hilariously underwhelming that it makes the whole search even funnier.

At just 84 to 176 pages, depending on the edition, H. G. Wells' The Time Machine is a Victorian-era predecessor to Back to the Future. The novella follows an eccentric English scientist known only as the Time Traveller, who builds a machine capable of traveling through time. Curious about humanity's future, he journeys to the year 802,701, where he encounters the Eloi, a seemingly carefree society living among the remnants of an advanced civilization. However, the world he discovers is far more complicated than it first appears, forcing him to reconsider what humanity’s future might look like.

Released during the Second Industrial Revolution, The Time Machine explores how technology shapes humanity and its relationship with nature. While these forces continue to intersect in the 21st century, seeing them through a late 19th-century perspective offers a fascinating glimpse into Victorian anxieties about progress. During this period, technological advancement was often seen as the key to Britain's continued dominance, reflecting the belief that humanity would only grow smarter, stronger, and more powerful. However, the Time Traveller's journey challenges that assumption. The book shows that human evolution has no guaranteed endpoint, and reaching what seems like the pinnacle of progress doesn't mean humanity's future will be any brighter.

Four ships, four completely different reasons to be up there at all. Here is the one that has your seat, what flying with them would cost you, and what it would give back.

You belong on the fastest piece of junk in the galaxy, with a crew that took the job for the payday and then quietly stopped caring about the payday. Nothing on the Falcon has ever gone according to plan, and everybody aboard prefers it that way.

You belong with the crew that turned a tiny cell of misfits into an actual rebellion. The Ghost is a home before it is a ship, and everybody who boards it arrived with something broken that the rest of them decided to look after.

You belong with the four kids who found a buried ship, launched it by accident and are now extremely lost in a galaxy that eats people like them. Nobody here knows what they are doing, and that turns out to be the fun of it.

You belong in the quietest ship in the galaxy, with one small passenger and a code you have never explained to anybody. You told yourself this was a job, and then it stopped being a job somewhere around the second week.

At roughly 370 pages, Andy Weir's The Martian is longer than some entries on this list, but its brisk pace—and the light, conversational tone from the lead character himself—makes it easy to keep turning pages. Mark Watney is on NASA's Ares 3 mission when a dust storm forces the crew to abandon Mars. An accident leaves him injured and separated from the others, who assume he is dead and head home. When Mark wakes up, he finds himself alone, with limited supplies, a damaged spacesuit, and no way to contact Earth. His only chance is to use his scientific knowledge to solve problems and find a way back.

The setup may sound like a straightforward survival thriller, but Weir gives the story an emotional purpose. Mark's resourcefulness keeps him alive, while the rescue effort shows how far people will go for someone they refuse to abandon. Back on Earth, NASA must decide whether another mission and its crew should be put at risk to bring him home. That dilemma gives the novel its heart. For all its science and engineering, The Martian comes down to one moral lesson: one person's life matters, even when saving it demands sacrifice. It's a reminder that survival is less of a solo achievement and more about people refusing to give up on you.

Reading is a crime in Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451—arguably treated as more serious than murder. Anyone caught hiding, distributing, or even reading a book risks imprisonment. Firemen have an unusual job in this society: instead of putting out fires, they set books alight. Guy Montag has never questioned this arrangement until he meets Clarisse, a young neighbor whose curiosity about life challenges everything he has accepted as normal. His doubts deepen after he witnesses a woman choose to die with her books rather than surrender them. The encounter forces him to reconsider his job and the society he has served.

Depending on the edition, Fahrenheit 451 runs between 156 and 256 pages, but Bradbury packs a chillingly prophetic vision into that length. Published in the 1950s, the novel imagines a society that feels uncomfortably familiar today, from attempts to ban books deemed "controversial" to people spending hours glued to their phone screens. It also raises concerns about political forces seeking to silence criticism and discourage independent thought. Bradbury's warning is not simply that technology can distract people from the world. In the wrong hands, it can also become a tool for enforcing conformity, keeping the public occupied while those in power avoid scrutiny. Anyone who challenges that system risks consequences.

#3440. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3436. 34 Years After Aladdin Hit Cinemas, Disney Confirms Bizarre New Lore

Aladdin has always been one of Disney’s most beloved classic films and continues to draw in both new and returning fans, even decades after its release. However, what many viewers may not know is that there’s a new comic book installment that continues the series while expanding the universe in unexpected ways.

Published by Dynamite Entertainment on November 4, 2026, Aladdin #4 shares a bizarre development that fans likely didn’t see coming. For just a short moment, it takes the iconic Genie somewhere he has never been before, crossing paths with unlikely characters that are far removed from Agrabah, and it’s not only entertaining, but also undeniably fitting for Genie.

The Aladdin comics currently have four issues, all of which are written by James III and illustrated by Agnese Eterno. The fourth and most recent issue follows the people of Agrabah after the city is trapped inside a glass bottle. With panic spreading among citizens, Princess Jasmine steps up to take charge while Aladdin and Genie search for a way to save their home from the outside.

While the central conflict centers on the city’s predicament, the issue also includes a quick, unexpected development involving Genie that reveals the universe Aladdin takes placein is far bigger than anyone expected. One page early in the issue follows Genie as he finds himself careening through the cosmos, where he comes into contact with extraterrestrial life in a spaceship as he passes by.

The moment is a quick, humorous detour that doesn’t have a major impact on the issue’s central plot, but it does establish that the universe is much larger than anyone imagined. Until now, Aladdin has only been known for magic, grand kingdoms, and fantastical adventures rather than anything sci-fi-related.

That said, the development is also extremely fitting for Genie, given that he has always existed beyond the bounds of the ordinary. After Aladdin’s wish to set him free, it’s only natural that Genie would have unexpected adventures and encounters, even if those take place somewhere out in the cosmos. In fact, this small moment arguably encapsulates Genie’s legacy in the franchise as limitless and full of possibility.

Even before being freed from the lamp, Genie had always existed somewhere beyond traditional limitations, making him an extraordinary character, even in a world filled with sorcerers and magic flying carpets. Even his personality adds to how boundless he truly feels, and this subversive portrayal reflects Disney’s history as well, because Genie defied the conventions of his time.

Genie stood out from other Disney characters for a variety of reasons. Brought to life by the legendary Robin Williams, Genie constantly incorporated contemporary references and celebrity impressions, along with plenty of fourth-wall breaks and improvised performances. At the time, Disney was still known for classic fairy tales and a more traditional storytelling approach, making Genie’s character completely revolutionary.

One of Disney's most beloved movies gets a five-chapter prequel spinoff that expands a villain's backstory right before the events of the film.

Beyond that, he was far from just a simple comic-relief character. Genie had a deeply meaningful arc surrounding his desire for freedom, driving him to enter a transactional agreement with Aladdin that ultimately led to the film’s emotional climax when Genie’s cuffs were finally gone, allowing him to live as he wished.

This journey makes Genie feel truly larger-than-life, and his experiences after the film continue to mirror that. While Genie’s brief encounter with alien life might be little more than a passing moment in the latest comic, it truly does capture his character’s lasting appeal and seemingly limitless reach within the story. Even decades after he was introduced in Disney’s Aladdin, Genie continues to defy expectations and push the boundaries of every story he’s in.

#3434. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3432. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

Terrence has a backup plan if Hollywood flips on its head ... when we caught up with him in New York City last week, he floated a run for president.

#3429. Denzel Washington's Sci-Fi Crime Thriller 'Déjà Vu' Is 'Minority Report' Meets 'Looper'

If you’re in the mood for a fast-paced action thriller that goes in a surprising speculative direction, then you need to jump over to Tubi for one of Denzel Washington's greatest on-screen exploits. Currently free to stream on the platform is Déjà Vu, a post-9/11, post-Hurricane Katrina thriller that speaks to nationwide fears at the time, infusing them with a sci-fi twist that elevates the film to be more than just your average action flick. If it's been a few years, now is the perfect time to revisit the picture, as November marks the 20th anniversary of this Tony Scott-directed classic.

Like most of his features, Déjà Vu boasts Scott's signature style of kinetic energy and hyper-focused characters, as ATF agent Doug Carlin (Washington) struggles to catch a domestic terrorist, Carroll Oerstadt (Jim Caviezel), a self-appointed "patriot" who bombed a New Orleans ferry containing U.S. Navy sailors and their families. Soon after the attack, FBI agent Paul Pryzwarra (Val Kilmer) brings Carlin aboard his specialized task force centered around a secret government project that may help catch the killer. As it turns out, scientists have accidentally created a window in time—a window that offers Carlin the chance to stop the tragedy before it occurs. The only problem is that they can only look back just over four days, and those days pass by in real time with no ability to rewind. With little else to do but study the life of victim Claire Kuchever (Paula Patton), Carlin comes to recognize both the killer and his role in stopping him.

Déjà Vu is one of those action-thrillers that has you on the edge of your seat the entire time. Although the worst of it has already happened, the film treads in reverse as it attempts to put all the pieces together, intelligently weaving a narrative where the past and present intersect. This, naturally, leads to some interesting philosophical, as well as theological, conundrums, as Carlin and the team debate the ethics of such government surveillance (after the conspiratorial Enemy of the State, but before The Dark Knight did the same) and the moral uncertainty that arises from operating a window into the past: If God allows such a window to exist, is it not so that Carlin and company can then use it to not just solve a murder, but perhaps prevent one? These are the questions that anchor Déjà Vu, presenting the audience with some complex choices as time rapidly slips through the hourglass and the window into the recent past moves closer to the present tragedy.

Second watches are for catching everything you were too stressed to notice the first time.

Of all five collaborations between Washington and Scott, Déjà Vu is perhaps the most creatively engaging. (Yes, that's even considering the truly remarkable Man on Fire.) The 2006 thriller uses Scott's distinct visual style to go beyond the simple action thriller, bending genre and making way-out speculative concepts palatable for standard action audiences. At the same time, Washington toes the line between romance and duty as he begins to fall for the woman who, in his timeline, is already dead. It's a brilliant concept with impeccable execution that goes beyond the pair's usual brand of grounded, fast-paced thrillers.

As such, Déjà Vu offers the viewer plenty of thrills, chills, and philosophical pondering, and pits them against a ticking clock that screams "already, but not yet." It's an exceptional film that perfectly encapsulates the anxieties of early 2000s America while not grounding itself in them so deeply that it feels outdated or outpaced. Indeed, it's the type of film that they don't seem to make anymore—a mid-budget thriller with a stacked cast and great thematic potential—and that's a real shame. Tony Scott was a visionary filmmaker who never let genre (or anything, really) constrain his vision, and with Denzel Washington in the leading role, Déjà Vu is still just as great today as it was 20 years ago.

Déjà Vu is available for streaming on Tubi.

#3427. 10 Greatest Opening Lines In Sci-Fi Movie History, Ranked

Without a doubt, science-fiction movies can have some of the greatest and most visually stunning opening sequences in cinematic history. However, sometimes what makes these openings so memorable can be what is heard and/or read just as much as what is shown on screen. Additionally, some of the best lines in a sci-fi movie can be the ones we get right off the bat.

Typically used to introduce a universe, overarching concepts, themes, or most important ideas, the opening lines in a sci-fi movie can be some of its most important and/or memorable. Frequently, the first lines we get are written and shown as introductory text rather than spoken aloud (though sometimes it's both). These can be warnings about dark futures, explanations for major cosmic concepts, the time and setting, chosen figures, and even crucial dreams.

Keeping that in mind, here's a ranking of 10 of the greatest opening lines in sci-fi movie history, ranked from great to the absolute greatest of all time.

Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982) immediately establishes its setting and dystopian future via critical opening text that immediately gets audiences oriented to this world and current status quo. Explaining the creation of replicants by the Tyrell Corporation, the introduction is incredibly efficient as we're brought into the movie's primary conflict before we even meet Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard. The audience can quickly understand that this is a world where replicants are being hunted and considered illegal on Earth.

Kicking off the first-ever live-action Transformers franchise, Michael Bay's 2007 movie opens with the introduction of the AllSpark, the mysterious object that created all life on Cybertron (and the movie's major MacGuffin responsible for the conflict between the Autobots and Decepticons on Earth).

However, what makes this opening so memorable is that the nature and history of the AllSpark is narrated by Optimus Prime himself, who's voiced by the late, great Peter Cullen. As such, there's something inherently special about hearing Prime's first-ever lines of live-action dialogue from the same actor who first brought him to life in the original 80s animated series.

James Cameron's first Avatar movie opens with Sam Worthington's Jake Sully narrating his dreams. Well before he even sets foot on Pandora and takes control of his late brother's Na'vi avatar, Jake was dreaming of flying over jungles and embracing the feeling of freedom before inevitably waking up to a much harsher reality.

Ultimately, the line is even better in retrospect once the full movie is watched, seeing as how Jake very much turns those dreams into a reality that both includes and stretches well beyond those dreams he had back on Earth. It's a simple opening, yet one that carries great meaning as both the franchise and Jake's journey continue to expand in the Avatar franchise.

Continuing with more James Cameron, his first Terminator movie wastes no time establishing the horrifying future awaiting humanity with some grim opening text detailing the eventual rise of the machines under Skynet following the brutal aftermath of nuclear war. Like with the previous examples, the opening text is brilliantly efficient yet compelling as the movie's overall time-traveling premise is set up, kicking off one of the most popular sci-fi franchises of all time.

Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) takes a very unconventional yet brilliant approach to its opening, which is likely why it's still considered one of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time today.

Following the film's iconic overture and visuals showing the sun, Earth, and moon in alignment, we get the simple opening title card that reads "Dawn of Man", which is all that's needed to establish the movie's initial prehistoric setting. Focusing on a group of ape-like hominids and their encounter with the alien black monolith, the movie's opening suggests that it was this otherworldly experience that influenced and sparked the evolution of humanity itself before jumping millions of years forward to the movie's present.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Before audiences fully understand the rules and world featured in The Matrix (1999), the movie opens with a recorded telephone conversation between Trinity and Cypher, confirming that their leader, Morpheus, believes a man named Neo is "The One." It's a fascinating way to kick off the movie by setting up its destined "Chosen One" before anything else, one that sets up major questions and mysteries that eventually get answered as Neo himself learns more about the true nature of the false reality he lives in and his true role and destiny within it.

Denis Villeneuve's first Dune movie opens with an anonymous Sardaukar priest speaking in the low bass tones of his own language, with the on-screen translation reading: "Dreams are messages from the deep," immediately establishing the importance of Paul Atreides' prophetic dreams and destiny as the Kwisatz Haderach, taking the mantle of the Fremen messiah Lisan al-Gaib, and becoming the galaxy's next emperor of the Imperium. Followed by Chani's narration introducing the crucially central world of Arrakis and its beauty, audiences are immediately drawn into the movie and its core themes.

Celebrating its 20th anniversary this year, Christopher Nolan's The Prestige begins as a psychological mystery thriller that gradually unveils its major sci-fi elements as the movie progresses. However, its opening line is unequivocally the movie's best, encouraging viewers to examine the movie and pieces of the puzzle as closely as they can, while also highlighting the movie's major themes of deception, perception, and the nature of illusion itself.

The Prestige challenges audiences to distinguish between what they're seeing and what's actually happening, with the full trick and major misdirects not being revealed at the very end. Thanks to its brilliantly unique and intentional narrative construction, the opening line is certainly one of the greatest of all time.

Few opening narrations are as recognizable or as memorable as the classic Star Trek monologue declaring space as the final frontier and the mission of the USS Enterprise. While it's most closely associated with the opening themes of the television series, the narration (and variants of it) have appeared in movies as well, including 2009's Star Trek reboot and its sequels starring Chris Pine, Zoe Saldaña, and Zachary Quinto.

Setting the perfect tone and themes of galactic exploration, discovery, and adventure, these opening words have come to represent decades of excellent sci-fi storytelling across shows and movies alike, making it one of the most timeless and iconic opening lines in all of sci-fi (except for one).

It's difficult to imagine any sci-fi movie opening greater or more iconic than Star Wars' opening text: "a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away." Before the opening crawl even begins, George Lucas establishes that audiences are about to experience something resembling a modern cosmic fairy tale rather than an outright sci-fi epic.

This memorable text is so brilliant in that it separates Star Wars from traditional science fiction. Despite all of its spaceships, robots, lightsabers, and futuristic technology, the franchise is fundamentally a fantasy epic with its peak hero and villain archetypes, supernatural powers, and overarching themes of destiny, good vs. evil, oppression, rebellion, and more. The opening line communicates that distinction immediately, inviting audiences into a universe that feels both futuristic and timeless (and it's a huge part of what has given Star Wars its enduring appeal for generations).

Nearly 50 years later, the key Star Wars phrase remains instantly recognizable, so much so that it's arguably the greatest invitation into any sci-fi movie world ever.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3420. Ridley Scott's Apple TV Crime Thriller Is a 10/10 Binge-Watch

A crime series needs certain qualities to work. Of course, there have to be twisty plots, plenty of exciting and suspenseful moments, and characters that you become instantly drawn to. Recent shows like True Detective, Task, and MobLand have all introduced viewers to thrilling episodes that provide an inside look at dark, mysterious criminal underworlds. One series in particular flew under the radar when it was released, but remains every bit as worthy of a binge-watch as the other shows in this genre.

The Ridley Scott-produced drama Dope Thief premiered on Apple TV in March 2025. Over a succinct eight episodes, the Peter Craig-created series never shies away from creating an intense and brutally violent yet completely captivating story. The series was adapted from a 2009 novel by Dennis Tafoya, and follows two best friends named Manny Carvalho (Wagner Moura) and Ray Driscoll (Brian Tyree Henry), who are trying to survive on the rough streets of Philadelphia. They've created a small-time robbery scheme where they pose as DEA agents and steal from local drug dealers.

After you watch 'Dope Thief,' go back and watch these shows!

Their con works pretty well until they take on a job that brings their whole lives crashing down. Even though there are plenty of red flags from the start, Ray and Manny rob a drug operation that is actually already being surveilled by real DEA officers. From there, the two men fall deeper and deeper into a massive criminal enterprise that puts them in danger at every turn. Can Manny and Ray outrun their fates, and will their friendship survive the danger that's coming for them? Each episode is fast-paced and drama-packed, but Dope Thief also manages to infuse its story with a wry humor that makes all the bloodshed a tiny bit easier to stomach.

Dope Thief stands apart from other crime shows because of its impressive blend of genres. One moment, you'll be covering your eyes at the violence, while a moment later, you'll be chuckling at the silly antics Manny and Ray are forced to perform to escape danger. Despite the humor and levity, Dope Thief never shies away from emphasizing the story's high-stakes circumstances. The series also impressively emphasizes the importance of found family. The bonds between many characters are compelling and authentic, and although most aren't related by blood, their connections are just as powerful. Dope Thief also successfully portrays the long-lasting effects of trauma and the heartbreak of knowing someone struggling with addiction, weaving these elements to make each episode better than the last.

Much of Dope Thief's success is tied to Wagner and Henry's performances. Their chemistry is both electric and effortless, and each actor proves why they're considered among the best in the industry right now. It's no surprise that Henry was nominated for an Emmy for his work as Ray. Marin Ireland is also incredible as Mina, a beautifully broken undercover agent who becomes entangled in Ray and Manny's lives. We'd be remiss if we didn't mention the stellar performances of Kate Mulgrew as Ray's tough-as-nails adoptive mother and Ving Rhames as Ray's gruff, embattled father.

For more than a year, fans wondered if there would be future episodes of Dope Thief. However, a few weeks ago, it was announced that Apple TV wouldn't be moving forward with the series. Although it's a shame that there'll be no Season 2, you should still check out this exceptional show. With an impressive 86% Rotten Tomatoes score and edge-of-your-seat storytelling, Dope Thief is the perfect addition to the crime thriller genre.

#3417. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has already taken the literary world by storm, and Matt Dinniman's wildly popular LitRPG series is now preparing to conquer tabletops with its highly anticipated role-playing game. With the official Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG preparing for its wider retail launch, fans have already created an incredible resource that could make their adventures through the World Dungeon way easier. Point Mongo is a completely free, community-driven website dedicated to homebrew content for Renegade Game Studios' upcoming tabletop RPG, offering players and game masters an expanding collection of tools, ideas, and original creations.

The name itself is a reference to Point Mongo, a town featured on the sixth floor of the World Dungeon in The Butcher's Masquerade (Book 5). Princess Donut takes control of the settlement, which becomes an important location during Carl and Donut's adventures through the Hunting Grounds.

The website is equally ambitious, having already surpassed 1,000 entries across 30 categories, with contributions from approximately 150 community members. Its enormous library covers practically everything players might need to expand their campaigns, including custom races, classes, magical items, monsters, bosses, spells, pets, quests, and even entire dungeon environments.

Point Mongo is also entirely community-supported, with users encouraged to submit original creations and help complete missing statistics for existing entries. Everything is freely accessible without requiring an account or subscription, and the project is unofficial and unaffiliated with Renegade Game Studios.

The website has already received an enthusiastic reception among RPG fans on Reddit. With new content being added regularly, Point Mongo could quickly become one of the most valuable free resources for Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG players, particularly those hoping to create their own unforgettable stories within Matt Dinniman's universe.

#3409. The Best Fantasy Book You Haven't Read Hits Harder Today Than Ever Before

We live in a complex time, entertainment-wise. AI is a genuine risk to art forms of all types, and large businesses are taking over each other, acting suspiciously like a monopoly. That's without mentioning how streaming keeps changing the name of the game for everyone and everything, and we keep finding entertainment in efforts that appeal to the lowest common denominator.

The writing was on the wall for years, and many visionary authors predicted the future of the entertainment industry with such accuracy that it's outright frightening. Then there are those who took it to the extreme, satirizing the very concept of what we find entertaining and offering a scathing view of it: that's exactly what Matthew Woodring Stover did in his underrated 1997 gem, Heroes Die. Set in a bleak version of the future, this science-fantasy tale features a wildly creative and unforgiving critique of corporate media and the audience's obsession with spectacle that makes it all the more powerful today.

Heroes Die is set in a dystopian, 23rd-century Earth where society is organized in strict castes and corporations run things following a plague outbreak that collapsed the previous governments. Coexisting with reality is Overworld, a parallel dimension of fantastical creatures and magic, where warring empires wreak havoc. Corporations have found a way to sell experiences to people on Earth by hiring actors from Earth to assume personas on Overworld and go on real, high-stakes adventures, which are then sold to the audience as an immersive, first-person experience.

The plot centers on Hari Michaelson, an actor who assumes the ruthless identity of Caine in Overworld, known as the Blade of Tyshalle across the city of Ankhana. When his estranged wife, Pallas Ri, is captured in Ankhana and her connection to Earth is severed, Hari agrees to go into Overworld as Caine to rescue her. However, he must also kill the ruling emperor per the request of the studio executives, as the ongoing succession crisis and potential civil war would make for a great setting for future adventures.

The world of Heroes Die is ruthless and bleak, grimdark literature at its finest. This version of Earth is pure nightmare fuel, with corporations controlling nearly every aspect of culture, and therefore everyday life. Overworld isn't much better, as the violent, survival-of-the-fittest credo makes for a dangerous and perennially brutal way of life. Stover perfectly blends genres, embracing all the aesthetics and themes of fantasy and updating them through a distinct sci-fi lens. Indeed, the book exists right in the middle, never giving in to one or the other.

From the very beginning, the world of Heroes Die feels like an infinitely darker and exaggerated yet uncomfortably familiar version of our current situation. Sure, we don't have a fantasy alternate reality coexisting with ours (that we know of), but thematically and in everything that concerns Earth, this dystopia feels dangerously possible. For starters, there's the mysterious plague that collapsed the previous structures, which in a post-COVID world feels not only feasible but perhaps inevitable. Then, there's the fact that corporations have taken over and dictate society's way of life, shaping it through the ruthless entertainment system they pioneered and control. Movies like Network have also toyed with this idea — that corporations are our new religion and can easily manipulate us — but Heroes Die makes it feel all the more real because it makes the entertainment so enticing.

Indeed, the book makes us complicit in the violence it's critiquing. Stover doesn't pull back with the guts and gore: Heroes Die features extreme sequences of intense and unforgiving violence, some of which verge on the cruel and are actively tough to read through. Yet, we remain hooked to the page, not only because of his gift as a wordsmith, but because the world he created is as engaging and alluring as it is repulsive. Think of this book as a literary version of Michael Haneke's Funny Games: it's openly judging you for partaking in the violence it's depicting, even daring, wanting you to turn away, but you just... don't. Our collective need for sensationalism is crucial here, and Stover understands and weaponizes it.

Here is where the book's takedown of modern entertainment values rings the strongest. Heroes Die is a scathing denunciation of what we find entertaining and where we place value. It not only predicted the rise of reality television as a dominant cultural force, but it also accurately guessed that someone, somewhere, at some point in time, would find a way to sell violence as amusement. Like some of its spiritual siblings, including Stephen King's The Running Man, Heroes Die sadly acknowledges that we find degradation fun, especially if we find a way to justify our enjoyment. "It's all staged" and "none of it is true" are constant reminders that real people are engaging in those acts, whether by greed, need, or both.

Books like Heroes Die take a mundane concept (a man willing to rescue his wife while dealing with corporate interests) and introduce an out-of-this-world concept to make it more engaging. Yet, the struggle is still familiar and, to many, relatable. At its core, the book is about what we're willing to do for someone we care about, but it's also about how we survive in a world dictated by profit and loss, and what we're willing to sacrifice to do it. In a way, it says that violence is not only inevitable, but also an inherent part of us, to the point where we can't even be rid of it by escaping into a fantasy world of gods and emperors. In fact, it's so natural to us that we're not only prone to it, but also compelled by it. Harrowingly, violence here is both the question and the answer, the crime and the punishment. By merely existing, Heroes Die is proving its point.

#3408. iOS 27.2’s clever new Messages feature can be tailored to your needs

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a convenient new Messages feature called ‘Suggested Actions.’ Here’s how you can customize the feature to your liking.

If your iPhone is running iOS 27.2, you might have noticed a handy addition in the Messages app.

Whenever a message contains actionable information—an event you might want to add to your calendar, or todo you need reminding of—Messages will add a ‘Suggested Action’ right below the relevant message.

Using these new suggestions, with a quick tap you can turn the message into an action. And they’re so small and unobtrusive in the UI that they don’t clutter up the app at all.

But depending on your needs, you might want to enable or disable some of these suggestions. And Apple lets you do that with a surprising level of granularity.

Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages -> Suggested Actions you’ll find customization options for the feature.

There are five different types of suggestions that can be enabled or disabled in Settings. By default, all five are enabled.

I’m planning to leave all five enabled, because I’ve found the feature a useful addition. But it’s great to see Apple offer a refreshing level of control like this right off the bat.

Note: Suggested Actions are powered by Apple Intelligence, so you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get the feature.

#3405. ChatGPT and Work are merging soon, while ChatGPT Classic retires in January

Users who still rely on the ChatGPT Classic app were greeted today with a message informing them that the app will soon be retired. Separately, OpenAI is also preparing to merge ChatGPT and Work into a single interface. Here are the details.

A few months ago, OpenAI released a new ChatGPT desktop app, which brought ChatGPT, Work, and Codex under a single interface. As a result, the regular ChatGPT app was renamed ChatGPT Classic.

The move proved controversial for two reasons. First, OpenAI replaced the native macOS app with an Electron-based version. Second, the new interface was extremely confusing, making it difficult to access regular ChatGPT conversations or even distinguish between ChatGPT, Work, and Codex.

OpenAI was quick to address some of the complaints, restoring direct access to conversations via a prominent Chat and Work toggle at the top of the window, along with a sidebar menu for switching between ChatGPT and Codex. The company has since introduced other changes to make the app easier to use.

The ChatGPT Classic app, on the other hand, remained largely untouched and became increasingly less reliable as OpenAI released new models that were more tightly integrated with features exclusive to the new app, such as the ability to select different reasoning effort levels.

And as much as it felt like the writing had been on the wall for its demise, now we have a date. According to a new message displayed to users when they open ChatGPT Classic, the app will officially be retired on January 30, 2027.

“This app will retire on January 30, 2027. Get the latest features in the new ChatGPT app. Your full chat history comes with you, so you can pick up where you left off.”

Clicking on the banner leads users to the ChatGPT downloads page, where they can download the latest version of the desktop app.

Meanwhile, OpenAI is informing users that it will begin testing a combined Chat and Work experience in the coming weeks.

The announcement comes a few months after OpenAI president Greg Brockman acknowledged that the new ChatGPT interface was “kind of a mess,” and said the company hoped to eliminate the Work tab by the end of the year, with its functionality becoming part of the regular ChatGPT experience.

Now, in an email sent to users, OpenAI explains that the test will start with a small group of users, who will be able to access ChatGPT’s conversational features and Work’s more advanced capabilities from the same interface:

This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.

As part of the transition, OpenAI also plans to introduce a shared usage allowance for ChatGPT and Codex, replacing their separate limits.

According to the company, “most users won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do today.” OpenAI adds that “usage will depend on model and task, with more advanced models and complex tasks using more of your allowance. Unlimited Instant is included in your plan and will not draw from your usage.”
